value: dominant power fell from waking 31.4 +/- 1.4 dB to 23.1 +/- 1.5 dB (stage 2), 24.7 +/- 1.4 dB (stage 4) and 24.3 +/- 1.3 dB (REM); 2-4 cpm activity fell from 90.8 +/- 3.2% awake to 64.6 +/- 7.6% (stage 2) and 57.5 +/- 5.5% (stage 4), not significantly vs REM (74.1 +/- 5.4%)
range: electrogastrogram over 20-min segments under polysomnography; no significant differences between sleep stages; emptying itself was not measured
citation: Elsenbruch S, Orr WC, Harnish MJ, Chen JD 1999, Sleep 22:453-458; doi:10.1093/sleep/22.4.453; pmid:10389221

parameter: gastric contraction amplitude by sleep depth
value: the amplitude of gastric contractions decreased with depth of sleep (light sleep N2 vs deep sleep N3; P<0.05); progression through the small intestine did not change with depth of sleep
range: pilot; ingestible electromagnetic capsules (3D-Transit) with polysomnography; emptying not measured as a rate
citation: Haase AM, Fallet S, Otto M, Scott SM, Schlageter V, Krogh K 2015, Clin Exp Gastroenterol 8:327-332; doi:10.2147/ceg.s91964; pmid:26677340

parameter: gastric emptying during sleep (narrative review)
value: gastric emptying is slow during sleep but REM sleep is associated with faster gastric emptying; gastrointestinal function markedly reduced most of the time during sleep
range: narrative review in Portuguese with an English abstract; no emptying rate given
citation: Dantas RO, Aben-Athar CG 2002, Arq Gastroenterol 39:55-59; doi:10.1590/s0004-28032002000100010; pmid:12184167

parameter: factor by which sleep slows the rise of hunger (the decay of post-absorptive satiety) per hour, against quiet wakefulness at the same time since the last meal
range: named by Plan 11c (ruling 11c-21, F_sleep); the harvested sources give the direction only: morning hunger after a night awake exceeds that after a night asleep at the same fast (Schmid 2008, Hogenkamp 2013), sleep restriction raises hunger 13.4 mm (Zhu 2019), and a circadian peak-to-trough difference of 17% of the mean, trough 07:50 (Scheer 2013); none states a per-hour rate, and a bedtime snack's satiety is gone by morning (Lay 2018)

parameter: gastric emptying rate or half-time of a meal while asleep
range: no measurement found in the 2026-10-08 Europe PMC search; slowing is inferred from evening-meal half-times taken awake (Goo 1987, evening meal emptying time +53.6%, measured from 8 PM), electrogastrography (Elsenbruch 1999), contraction amplitude (Haase 2015) and a narrative review (Dantas 2002)

parameter: appetite-hormone response to an acute bout of exercise (pooled AUC effect sizes) (the reading that PYY and GLP-1 rise, against Douglas 2016 in overweight or obese adults)
value: acylated ghrelin suppressed: Cohen's d -0.20 (95% CI -0.373 to -0.027), median decrease 16.5%; PYY raised: d 0.24 (95% CI 0.007 to 0.475), median increase 8.9%; GLP-1 raised: d 0.275 (95% CI -0.031 to 0.581), median increase 13%; PP raised: d 0.50 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.89), median increase 15%
range: 20 studies (28 trials), 241 participants (77.6% men); random effects for acylated ghrelin (18 studies, 25 trials) and PYY (8 studies, 14 trials), fixed effects for PP (4 studies, 5 trials) and GLP-1 (5 studies, 8 trials); no significant heterogeneity; publication bias detected for all analyses; no moderator variable (intensity, duration, mode, participant characteristics) moderated acylated ghrelin or PYY
population: healthy adults, mostly men, in acute laboratory exercise trials reporting AUC over more than three time points
citation: Schubert MM, Sabapathy S, Leveritt M, Desbrow B 2014, Sports Med 44:387-403; doi:10.1007/s40279-013-0120-3; pmid:24174308

parameter: acylated ghrelin, PYY and GLP-1 after acute exercise in overweight or obese adults (pooled) (the reading that PYY and GLP-1 do not rise in this population, against Schubert 2014)
value: acylated ghrelin AUC suppressed: pooled SMD -0.34 (95% CI -0.53 to -0.15); total PYY SMD 0.10 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.31); GLP-1 SMD -0.03 (95% CI -0.18 to 0.13); the acylated ghrelin reduction greater at higher mean BMI (metaregression slope -0.04 SMD per kg/m2, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.00)
range: 6 published studies, 73 participants (78% male), random effects
population: overweight or obese adults (mean BMI 30.6 kg/m2)
citation: Douglas JA, Deighton K, Atkinson JM et al 2016, J Obes 2016:2643625; doi:10.1155/2016/2643625; pmid:28116150

parameter: time course of hunger during and after intense exercise and its effect on the next meal (exercise-induced anorexia)
value: subjective hunger significantly suppressed during and after intense exercise sessions (P < 0.01) but the suppression was short-lived; no significant effect on the amount eaten at the test meal; intense exercise delayed the start of eating (P < 0.05); only the long-duration high-intensity session created a significant short-term negative energy balance relative to expenditure (P < 0.001)
range: two repeated-measures studies, three conditions each (control, low and high intensity; control, short and long duration at high intensity), randomly assigned; hunger by VAS and the time from the end of exercise to the volitional onset of eating; intake by a free-selection test meal and recorded for the next 2 days; the abstract gives no VAS magnitude and no duration in minutes
population: 23 healthy lean men (n = 11 and n = 12), Leeds University population
citation: King NA, Burley VJ, Blundell JE 1994, Eur J Clin Nutr 48:715-724; pmid:7835326

parameter: hunger and acylated ghrelin over 9 h after a 60-min run at 72% VO2max vs rest
value: acylated ghrelin AUC lower with exercise: 317 +/- 135 vs 510 +/- 186 pg.ml-1.3 h over the first 3 h and 917 +/- 342 vs 1,401 +/- 521 pg.ml-1.9 h over 9 h (means +/- SE; P < 0.05); hunger AUC lower over the first 3 h of the exercise trial (P = 0.013)
range: random crossover, two 9-h trials from 0800 after an overnight fast; run 0800-0900, test meal at 1100; hunger by visual scale; hunger magnitudes not in the abstract
citation: Broom DR, Stensel DJ, Bishop NC et al 2007, J Appl Physiol 102:2165-2171; doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00759.2006; pmid:17347386

parameter: hunger, acylated ghrelin and PYY during and after resistance vs aerobic exercise (exercise mode)
value: significant interaction effects (P < 0.05) indicating suppressed hunger and acylated ghrelin during aerobic and resistance exercise and increased PYY during aerobic exercise; 8-h PYY AUC control 1,411 +/- 110, resistance 1,381 +/- 97, aerobic 1,750 +/- 170 pg/ml 8 h
range: randomised crossover, three 8-h trials: 90-min free-weight lifting then 6.5 h rest; 60-min run then 7 h rest; 8 h rest; meals at 2 and 5 h; hunger magnitudes not in the abstract
population: 11 healthy male students (21.1 +/- 0.3 y, BMI 23.1 +/- 0.4 kg/m2, VO2max 62.1 +/- 1.8 ml/kg/min)
citation: Broom DR, Batterham RL, King JA, Stensel DJ 2009, Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 296:R29-R35; doi:10.1152/ajpregu.90706.2008; pmid:18987287

parameter: appetite, intake and acylated ghrelin after 60 min of self-paced brisk walking (low intensity: no suppression)
value: brisk walking (7.0 +/- 0.1 km/h) yielded a net energy expenditure of 2008 +/- 134 kJ yet did not significantly influence appetite, energy or macronutrient intake or acylated ghrelin during or after exercise (P > 0.05); no compensation, so a deficit of 1836 kJ (439 kcal) relative to control
range: randomised counterbalanced, two 8-h trials; ad libitum buffet meals at 1.5-2 and 5-5.5 h; appetite every 30 min
population: 14 healthy young men (21.9 +/- 0.5 y, BMI 23.4 +/- 0.6 kg/m2, VO2max 55.9 +/- 1.8 ml/kg/min)
citation: King JA, Wasse LK, Broom DR, Stensel DJ 2010, Med Sci Sports Exerc 42:485-492; doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181ba10c4; pmid:19952806

parameter: overall appetite over 8 h after 60 min of moderate-intensity treadmill exercise (59% peak VO2) vs rest, and its duration
value: main effect of trial: overall appetite lower in the exercise than the control trial (95% CI -3.1 to -0.5 mm, ES = 0.07, P = 0.01); trial-by-time interaction: lower at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 h (all ES >= 0.60, P <= 0.001); lower at 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 h (all ES >= 0.60, P <= 0.001); ad libitum energy intake at 7 h similar (95% CI -391 to 346 kJ, P = 0.90); delta acylated ghrelin not different (95% CI -5 to 3 pg/ml, P = 0.76)
range: randomised crossover, two 8-h trials; exercise at 0-1 h; standardised meals at 1.5 and 4 h; buffet at 7 h; overall appetite is the mean of hunger, satisfaction, fullness and prospective food consumption on 100-mm VAS every 30 min (satisfaction and fullness reverse-scored); lean -3.5 mm (ES 0.14) vs overweight/obese -0.1 mm (ES < 0.01), trial-by-group P = 0.01; overall appetite already lower in the exercise than the control trial at baseline (95% CI -11.2 to -0.4 mm, ES = 0.34, P = 0.04)
population: 47 healthy adults: 22 lean (11 female; 37.5 y; 22.4 kg/m2) and 25 overweight/obese (11 female; 45.0 y; 29.2 kg/m2)
citation: Douglas JA, King JA, Clayton DJ et al 2017, Int J Obes (Lond) 41:1737-1744; doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.181; pmid:28769121

parameter: duration of acute appetite suppression after a single bout, and its dependence on intensity (HIIT/SIT vs moderate continuous)
value: both HIIT/SIT and MICT suppressed appetite vs no-exercise control immediately post exercise, with no significant effect 30-90 min post exercise or in AUC values; HIIT/SIT suppressed hunger more than MICT 30-90 min post exercise (MD = -6.347 mm [-12.054, -0.639], p = 0.029); differences between HIIT/SIT and MICT immediately post exercise negligible
range: 13 randomised controlled studies to September 2021; VAS; the abstract gives no mean difference against control
citation: Hu M, Nie J, Lei OK, Shi Q, Kong Z 2023, Appetite 182:106427; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2022.106427; pmid:36565929

parameter: the intensity threshold and mode dependence of exercise-induced anorexia (narrative consensus)
value: subjective feelings of appetite transiently suppressed during exercise performed at or greater than 60% peak oxygen uptake; the change has been reported after resistance exercise but is less marked and is not observed consistently; Appetite perceptions typically return to resting control values within 30 to 60 min of exercise cessation
range: narrative review; studies mostly in lean, physically active men
citation: Dorling J, Broom DR, Burns SF et al 2018, Nutrients 10:1140; doi:10.3390/nu10091140; pmid:30131457

parameter: reproducibility and between-person variation of appetite suppression after a 60-min run at 70% peak VO2
value: exercise suppressed mean acylated ghrelin and appetite perceptions (all ES = 0.62-1.47, P < 0.001) and raised total PYY (ES = 1.49, P < 0.001) vs control; the SD of the change scores substantially greater in exercise than control; the two replicate responses correlated r = 0.54-0.82 (P <= 0.036); participant-by-condition interactions for all variables (P <= 0.053)
range: replicated crossover: two 60-min rest and two 60-min fasted treadmill-run conditions in randomised sequences; measured immediately before and after
citation: Goltz FR, Thackray AE, King JA et al 2018, Med Sci Sports Exerc 50:758-768; doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000001504; pmid:29240652

parameter: appetite, hormones and energy intake after acute exercise in overweight and obese adults (pooled)
value: hunger ES = -0.35; prospective food consumption ES = -0.26; fullness ES = 0.16; satiety ES = 0.15; acylated ghrelin ES = -0.73; insulin ES = -0.55 (nonsignificant); GLP-1 ES = 3.96 (nonsignificant); PYY ES = 0.24 (nonsignificant); relative energy intake ES = -0.54; absolute energy intake ES = -0.19
range: 19 studies (34 trials), random effects; an erratum is published (doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2025-0175)
population: people living with overweight or obesity
citation: Li N, Wu M, Li Y 2025, Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 35:540-556; doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2025-0078; pmid:40840552

parameter: gastric emptying during and after acute exercise vs rest (pooled), and its dependence on intensity and mode
value: volume emptied ES = 0.195 (95% CI -0.25 to 0.64); half-time ES = -0.109 (95% CI -0.66 to 0.44); oro-caecal transit time ES = 0.089 (95% CI -0.64 to 0.82), all non-significant; emptying faster at lower and slower at high exercise intensities; walking associated with faster and cycling with slower emptying; greater meal or fluid volume, higher osmolality and longer exercise duration associated with slower emptying
range: 20 studies (35 trials), 221 participants (157 men, 52 women, 12 unknown); Hedges' g, random effects; significant heterogeneity; mostly a liquid bolus given before exercise
citation: Horner KM, Schubert MM, Desbrow B, Byrne NM, King NA 2015, Sports Med 45:659-678; doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0285-4; pmid:25398225

parameter: dependence of the appetite-hormone response on exercise intensity (narrative)
value: changes in appetite-regulating hormones after acute exercise appear intensity-dependent, with increasing intensity leading to greater suppression of orexigenic signals and greater stimulation of anorexigenic signals; blood redistribution proposed as important for suppressing ghrelin
range: narrative review; no pooled estimate
population: healthy adults in acute exercise studies
citation: Hazell TJ, Islam H, Townsend LK, Schmale MS, Copeland JL 2016, Appetite 98:80-88; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2015.12.016; pmid:26721721

parameter: ad libitum energy intake after an acute bout of exercise vs rest, absolute and relative to the energy expended (pooled)
value: absolute energy intake: ES = 0.14 (95% CI -0.005 to 0.29), trivial; relative energy intake (creating an energy deficit): ES = -1.35 (95% CI -1.64 to -1.05), large; individuals tend not to compensate for the energy expended during exercise in the immediate hours after exercise
range: 29 studies, 51 trials (25 for relative intake); exercise 30-120 min at 36-81% VO2max; trials 2-14 h; ad libitum test meals 0-2 h post exercise; random effects
citation: Schubert MM, Desbrow B, Sabapathy S, Leveritt M 2013, Appetite 63:92-104; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2012.12.010; pmid:23274127

parameter: 24-h energy intake after a 90-min run vs no exercise (a large exercise deficit not compensated the same day)
value: participants expended 5324 kJ during exercise; 24-h energy intake control 17,191 kJ vs exercise 17,606 kJ, no compensatory increase; appetite and acylated ghrelin transiently suppressed and no different from control in the hours afterwards
range: randomised crossover; run at 68.8 +/- 0.8% VO2max then 8.5 h rest; ad libitum buffet meals; next-morning fasting sample and appetite ratings
citation: King JA, Miyashita M, Wasse LK, Stensel DJ 2010, Appetite 54:492-498; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2010.02.002; pmid:20152871

parameter: appetite and intake under equal same-day energy deficits created by exercise vs by food restriction
value: deficits by food restriction 4820 +/- 151 kJ and by exercise 4715 +/- 113 kJ; appetite and ad libitum energy intake responded in a compensatory fashion to food restriction yet were not influenced by exercise; acylated ghrelin rose and PYY3-36 fell under food restriction (trial x time P < 0.001 each), not under exercise
range: randomised counterbalanced, three 9-h trials; 90-min run at 70% VO2max at the start of the exercise trial, then 7.5 h rest; test meals at 2 and 4.75 h; buffet at 8 h
citation: King JA, Wasse LK, Ewens J et al 2011, J Clin Endocrinol Metab 96:1114-1121; doi:10.1210/jc.2010-2735; pmid:21270331

parameter: same-day compensation for land-based endurance exercise, and the exception of low-volume supramaximal exercise (narrative consensus)
value: a consensus among the majority of investigations that an acute bout of land-based endurance exercise does not stimulate compensatory increases in appetite and energy intake on the day of exercise; preliminary evidence that low-volume supramaximal exercise may increase appetite perceptions in the subsequent hours; the daily energy balance response to exercise primarily determined by the energy cost of exercise
range: narrative review
citation: Deighton K, Stensel DJ 2014, Proc Nutr Soc 73:352-358; doi:10.1017/S002966511400007X; pmid:24717417

parameter: post-exercise ad libitum energy intake after high-intensity or sprint interval vs moderate continuous exercise (pooled)
value: no difference in absolute energy intake for HIIE vs MICE (p = 0.54; 95% CI -0.14 to 0.26; 22 comparisons) or SIE vs MICE (p = 0.08; 95% CI -0.65 to 0.03; 6 comparisons), nor in relative energy intake (HIIE p = 0.97, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.10; SIE p = 0.28, 95% CI -1.03 to 0.06)
range: 17 studies, 28 pairwise comparisons, random effects; subgroup analyses (intake method, body mass, sex, volume, timing) non-significant
citation: Rossi PAQ, Panissa VLG, Silveira R et al 2022, Eur J Clin Nutr 76:929-942; doi:10.1038/s41430-021-01026-w; pmid:34675403

parameter: ad libitum energy intake after a single bout of water-based exercise vs no exercise, vs land, and by water temperature (pooled)
value: water vs control: +330 kJ (95% CI 118 to 542, P = 0.002); water vs land: 78 kJ (95% CI -176 to 334, P = 0.55); cold water (18-20 C) vs neutral (27-33 C): +719 kJ (95% CI 222 to 1215, P < 0.005)
range: 8 acute studies (water vs control), 5 (water vs land), 2 (two temperatures); fixed effects; appetite not meta-analysed because of heterogeneity
citation: Grigg MJ, Thake CD, Allgrove JE et al 2023, Appetite 180:106375; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2022.106375; pmid:36375602

parameter: ad libitum energy intake during or after acute cold or heat exposure vs thermoneutral, at rest or during exercise (pooled)
value: a small increase in energy intake in cold conditions (g = 0.44; p = 0.019) and a small decrease in hot conditions (g = -0.39; p = 0.022); the effect of exercise remains unclear
range: 13 randomised controlled trials (2 heat, 8 cold, 3 both)
citation: Millet J, Siracusa J, Tardo-Dino PE et al 2021, Nutrients 13:3424; doi:10.3390/nu13103424; pmid:34684424

parameter: compensatory change in energy intake and expenditure over 7-day periods in response to the energy imbalances of high (about 4 MJ/day) vs no exercise and high- vs low-fat diets (2 x 2), feeding ad libitum
value: mean daily expenditure 17.6 vs 11.5 MJ/day (P < 0.001) on high vs no exercise; the energy imbalances induced compensatory changes in energy balance over time of approximately 0.3-0.4 MJ/day (P < 0.05), from intake (approximately 0.2 MJ/day) and expenditure (approximately 0.35 MJ/day), small but persistent; EI 13.4 MJ/day on the high-fat vs 9.0 MJ/day on the low-fat diets
range: 2 x 2 randomised design (exercise x high- or low-fat diet), 7-day periods; intake weighed; expenditure by heart-rate monitoring
citation: Stubbs RJ, Hughes DA, Johnstone AM et al 2004, Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 286:R350-R358; doi:10.1152/ajpregu.00196.2003; pmid:14707013

parameter: fraction of an exercise-induced energy deficit compensated by intake over 14 days of ad libitum feeding
value: on average subjects compensated for about 30% of the exercise-induced energy deficit, the degree varying considerably among individuals; women EE 9.2, 11.6 and 13.7 MJ/d with EI 8.3, 8.6 and 9.9 MJ/d (P = 0.118); men EE 12.2, 14.0 and 16.7 MJ/d with EI 10.6, 11.6 and 12.0 MJ/d (P = 0.031) for no, moderate (1.5-2.0 MJ/d) and high (3.0-4.0 MJ/d) exercise; the authors state total compensation would take a matter of weeks
range: 16-day protocols, fed to balance on days 1-2, ad libitum on days 3-16 from a medium-fat diet of constant composition; EE by doubly labelled water; each subject studied three times
citation: Whybrow S, Hughes DA, Ritz P et al 2008, Br J Nutr 100:1109-1115; doi:10.1017/S0007114508968240; pmid:18377694

parameter: between-person variation in intake and hunger compensation over 12 weeks of supervised exercise
value: mean weight loss 3.7 +/- 3.6 kg as predicted, range -14.7 to +1.7 kg; compensators: energy intake +268.2 +/- 455.4 kcal/day and average daily hunger +6.9 +/- 11.4 mm; non-compensators: intake -130 +/- 485 kcal/day and hunger 0.4 +/- 9.6 mm/day
range: single-arm 12-week intervention, supervised exercise five times per week; compensators classed by actual vs predicted weight loss (NC 6.3 +/- 3.2 kg, C 1.5 +/- 2.5 kg)
population: 35 overweight and obese sedentary men and women (BMI 31.8 +/- 4.1 kg/m2; 39.6 +/- 11.0 y)
citation: King NA, Hopkins M, Caudwell P, Stubbs RJ, Blundell JE 2008, Int J Obes (Lond) 32:177-184; doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803712; pmid:17848941

parameter: rise in daily energy intake after 24 weeks of supervised exercise at two doses vs control (doubly labelled water)
value: energy intake rose by 90.7 kcal/d (95% CI 35.1, 146.4) at 8 kcal/kg/wk and 123.6 kcal/d (95% CI 64.5, 182.7) at 20 kcal/kg/wk vs -2.3 kcal/d (95% CI -58.0, 53.5) in control; weight compensation 1.5 kg (95% CI 0.9, 2.2) and 2.7 kg (95% CI 2.0, 3.5); RMR and non-exercise activity did not change differentially; participants with higher compensation reported increased appetite ratings
range: randomised controlled trial (E-MECHANIC), per-protocol n = 171 of 198 randomised; 72.5% women
population: adults with overweight or obesity (BMI 31.5 +/- 4.7 kg/m2)
citation: Martin CK, Johnson WD, Myers CA et al 2019, Am J Clin Nutr 110:583-592; doi:10.1093/ajcn/nqz054; pmid:31172175

parameter: energy compensation over 12 weeks of 1,500 vs 3,000 kcal/wk of exercise expenditure (compensation not proportional to dose)
value: compensation 943 (-164 to 2,050) and 1,007 (32 to 1,982) kcal/wk (mean, 95% CI; P >= 0.93), or 62.9% and 33.6% of exercise expenditure; resting metabolic rate and energy intake did not change; acylated ghrelin increased (P <= 0.02) and GLP-1 and food reinforcement decreased (P < 0.02)
range: randomised to 300 or 600 kcal per session, 5 days/wk, 12 wk; 14 and 15 completers; compensation from changes in body tissue energy stores
citation: Flack KD, Ufholz K, Johnson L, Fitzgerald JS, Roemmich JN 2018, Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol 315:R619-R626; doi:10.1152/ajpregu.00071.2018; pmid:29897822

parameter: total energy compensation (intake and expenditure together) for exercise energy expenditure across interventions, and its growth with duration
value: overall mean energy compensation 18% +/- 93%; for studies of about 80 weeks the compensation approached 84%; 48% of the variance explained by the interaction of initial fat mass, age and intervention duration; from 25 weeks onward compensation no longer differed by these predictors
range: 61 studies, 928 subjects; compensation = body energy change (fat and fat-free mass) over total exercise energy expenditure, so it includes intake and expenditure responses; sex, frequency, intensity and exercise dose were not significant predictors
citation: Riou ME, Jomphe-Tremblay S, Lamothe G et al 2015, Nutrients 7:3677-3704; doi:10.3390/nu7053677; pmid:25988763

parameter: daily energy intake and fasting hunger after exercise training vs no-exercise control (pooled)
value: in studies rated fair or good, no significant pre-post change in daily intake and a small but negligible (SMD < 0.20) post-intervention difference vs no-exercise control (five study arms; MD = 102 [1, 203] kcal); negligible-to-small pre-post increases in fasting hunger and dietary restraint
range: 48 articles; quality poor in 39, fair in 7, good in 2; median intervention 12 weeks; daily intake mostly self-reported
population: adults with overweight or obesity (median BMI 30.6 kg/m2)
citation: Beaulieu K, Blundell JE, van Baak MA et al 2021, Obes Rev 22 Suppl 4:e13251; doi:10.1111/obr.13251; pmid:33949089

parameter: total daily energy expenditure of military personnel in garrison and field training (doubly labelled water)
value: men: group means 13.0 to 29.8 MJ (3109-7131 kcal) per day, overall 19.3 +/- 2.7 MJ (4610 +/- 650 kcal) per day; women: 9.8 to 23.4 MJ (2332-5597 kcal) per day, overall 11.9 +/- 2.6 MJ (2850 +/- 620 kcal) per day; combat training higher than non-combat training or support; tended higher in the cold or at high altitude, not raised by hot weather
range: 424 men measured over an average 12.2 days (2.25-69); 77 women over an average 8.8 days (2.25-14); a compilation of measured groups
citation: Tharion WJ, Lieberman HR, Montain SJ et al 2005, Appetite 44:47-65; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2003.11.010; pmid:15604033

parameter: appetite during 72 h of strenuous activity (about 9.6 MJ/d activity expenditure) with limited sleep, energy-balanced vs energy-deficient, and the deficit needed to raise appetite
value: relative to sedentary REST: hunger, desire to eat and prospective consumption +26 (sd 40)%, +56 (sd 71)% and +28 (sd 34)% under the deficit diet and -55 (sd 25)%, -52 (sd 27)% and -54 (sd 21)% under the balanced diet; fullness +65 (sd 61)% under the balanced diet; regression predicted energy deficits of >= 25% would be required to elicit increases in appetite
range: randomised crossover after 1 sedentary balanced day; energy balance +18 (sd 20)% (BAL) and -43 (sd 9)% (DEF); slowed gastric emptying, raised anorexigenic hormones and lower fasting acylated ghrelin named as potential mechanisms of suppression; simulated sustained military operations (SUSOPS)
citation: Karl JP, Hatch-McChesney A, Allen JT et al 2021, Br J Nutr 126:1571-1584; doi:10.1017/S0007114521000131; pmid:33441218

parameter: energy intake and hunger across a 15-day military expedition in the cold with ample palatable food (intake compensation builds over days)
value: energy intake 15.3 +/- 2.1, 16.1 +/- 2.1 and 17.6 +/- 2.0 MJ for D1-5, D6-10 and D11-15 (p < .012), reaching neutral energy balance by D6-10; intake increased only in the mid-day (10:00-14:00) period; hunger and thirst increased only in the morning, higher in D11-15 than D1-5 (p < .009); body mass -1.13 +/- 1.42% and fat mass -19.5 +/- 15.6%
range: single-group field study; ~20-MJ daily bags of easy-to-use, highly palatable, familiar foods with multiple long breaks
citation: Charlot K, Chapelot D, Siracusa J et al 2021, Physiol Rep 9:e14591; doi:10.14814/phy2.14591; pmid:34057319

parameter: energy intake and hunger across a 14-day cold-weather military expedition in Greenland
value: energy expenditure 15 +/- 9 MJ/day, relatively constant; self-reported energy intake 17% higher in D8-D14 than D1-D7, giving a neutral energy balance; hunger scores (VAS) not significantly altered; body fat mass -1.0 +/- 0.7 kg (p < 0.001), body mass unchanged
range: single-group field study; easy-to-eat palatable foods in excess; expenditure by accelerometry, intake by diary
citation: Charlot K, Chapelot D, Colin P, Bourrilhon C 2020, Appl Physiol Nutr Metab 45:968-977; doi:10.1139/apnm-2019-0677; pmid:32187499

parameter: energy intake against expenditure on a 5-day field training exercise with rations, and the reasons given for underconsumption
value: energy expenditure 3,245 +/- 238 (CCAR) and 3,276 +/- 317 (FSR) kcal/day; intake 2,194 +/- 539 vs 1,914 +/- 611 kcal/day; energy deficit 32% +/- 12% vs 42% +/- 11%; the most commonly cited reasons for underconsumption: not liking the food, lack of time and lack of appetite
range: parallel single-blinded randomised trial; one ration per day (about 2,850-2,910 kcal provided); expenditure by doubly labelled water
citation: Dawson MA, Hatch-McChesney A, Ndou TV et al 2026, Mil Med usag134; doi:10.1093/milmed/usag134; pmid:41921503

parameter: underconsumption of operational rations in military training and field operations
value: military personnel in training and field operations often do not eat their rations in the amounts needed to meet their energy and nutrient requirements and consequently lose weight
range: committee report, 20 chapters; qualitative
citation: Institute of Medicine (US) Committee on Military Nutrition Research 1995, Not Eating Enough: Overcoming Underconsumption of Military Operational Rations, National Academies Press; doi:10.21236/ada300575; pmid:25121269

parameter: energy intake, hunger and balance over 7 days of a sedentary (1.4 x RMR) vs moderately active (1.8 x RMR) routine, feeding ad libitum
value: energy expenditure 9.7 vs 12.8 MJ/d (P < 0.01); energy intake 13.5 vs 14.4 MJ/d (P = 0.463); no regimen effect on hunger, appetite or body weight; cumulative energy balance by day 7 26.3 vs 11.1 MJ; a sedentary routine does not induce a compensatory reduction of intake
range: each subject studied twice, 7 days resident in a whole-body indirect calorimeter, medium-fat diet of constant composition
citation: Stubbs RJ, Hughes DA, Johnstone AM et al 2004, Am J Clin Nutr 79:62-69; doi:10.1093/ajcn/79.1.62; pmid:14684398

parameter: energy intake against physical activity across activity quintiles, and fat gain over 1 year (the low-activity uncoupling)
value: a positive relation between calculated energy intake and activity group except in the lowest quintile; the least-active group (15.7 +/- 9.9 min MVPA/d, 6062 +/- 1778 steps/d) gained the most fat mass over 1 y (1.7 +/- 0.3 kg); odds of gaining > 3% fat mass 1.8 to 3.8 times those of the middle activity group; a threshold for energy balance at 7116 steps/d
range: prospective cohort, measures every 3 months; intake calculated from body-composition change and energy expenditure
citation: Shook RP, Hand GA, Drenowatz C et al 2015, Am J Clin Nutr 102:1332-1338; doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.115360; pmid:26561620

parameter: energy intake across graded habitual physical activity levels (a J-shaped relation)
value: a significant curvilinear effect of graded activity level (low, medium, high, very high) on standardised energy intake (main effect F(3,21) = 3.57, P = 0.03; linear F = 5.79, P = 0.03; quadratic F = 8.10, P = 0.01); active individuals compensated better for high-energy preloads; appetite sensations and absolute energy intake did not differ consistently
range: 28 studies (14 cross-sectional, 14 exercise training); the J-curve from 10 cross-sectional studies, 8 on self-reported daily intake
citation: Beaulieu K, Hopkins M, Blundell J, Finlayson G 2016, Sports Med 46:1897-1919; doi:10.1007/s40279-016-0518-9; pmid:27002623

parameter: energy intake against occupational activity from sedentary to very heavy work (Mayer's uncoupling at low activity)
value: as Beaulieu 2016 reports it: daily energy expenditure and intake closely matched at higher levels of daily activity, but at low levels the coupling was lost, intake exceeding expenditure in those performing 'sedentary' or 'light' work; the primary's own numbers were not read
range: the primary has no abstract and its full text was not reachable at harvest (2026-10-08)
population: male jute-mill workers in West Bengal, sedentary to very heavy occupations
citation: Mayer J, Roy P, Mitra KP 1956, Am J Clin Nutr 4:169-175; doi:10.1093/ajcn/4.2.169; pmid:13302165

parameter: the pooled size, in mm VAS, of hunger suppression against a no-exercise control immediately after an acute aerobic bout, and its decay constant in minutes as a function of intensity
range: direction and duration family settled: suppression during and immediately after the bout (Hu 2023), absent 30-90 min after in that pooling but seen to 1.5 h at 59% peak VO2 (Douglas 2017) and in the 3-h hunger AUC after a 72% VO2max run (Broom 2007); Hu 2023's abstract gives a difference only against MICT (-6.347 mm); no source gives a time constant; a narrative 30-60 min return (Dorling 2018); Douglas 2017's main effect of trial -3.1 to -0.5 mm (ES 0.07) over 8 h, ES >= 0.60 at 0.5-1.5 h

parameter: the time constant, in days, over which intake compensation for a sustained rise in activity expenditure builds
range: readings at fixed horizons only: about 0.2 MJ/day of intake by 7 days (Stubbs 2004, AJP), about 30% of the deficit over 14 days (Whybrow 2008), 33.6-62.9% total compensation at 12 weeks (Flack 2018), an 18% mean rising toward 84% at about 80 weeks (Riou 2015, intake and expenditure together); no source fits a time constant
population: adults under weeks of added exercise, feeding ad libitum

parameter: appetite and intake under weeks of heavy daily manual labour with scarce or unpalatable food
range: the field studies run 3 to 15 days with ample (Charlot 2020, 2021) or ration-limited (Dawson 2026) food; the one controlled reading (Karl 2021) is 72 h; none covers weeks of labour under scarcity
population: people doing heavy physical work under food scarcity

parameter: acute energy intake reduction by viscous vs less viscous fibre (vote count; the companion of S0487's appetite reading)
value: more viscous fibres (e.g. pectins, beta-glucans and guar gum) reduced acute energy intake in 69% of comparisons vs 30% for less viscous fibres; overall effects on energy intake and body weight relatively small; distinct dose-response relationships not observed
range: systematic review of RCTs; effect rates as proportions of fibre-control comparisons: appetite n = 58, acute energy intake n = 26, long-term energy intake n = 38, body weight n = 66 comparisons; no pooled effect size; no certainty rating given
citation: Wanders AJ, van den Borne JJ, de Graaf C et al 2011, Obes Rev 12:724-739; doi:10.1111/j.1467-789X.2011.00895.x; pmid:21676152

parameter: post-meal energy intake under soluble-fibre supplementation by type, with the confidence intervals S1237 omits (the reading that only polydextrose's pooled effect excludes zero)
value: pooled Cohen's d on energy intake: guar gum -0.90 (95% CI -1.83, 0.03; I2 = 95.8%; random effects; n = 3); beta-glucan -0.44 (95% CI -0.91 to 0.04; I2 = 0%; fixed effects; n = 2); alginate -0.42 (95% CI -0.84, 0.01; I2 = 80.9%; random effects; n = 2); polydextrose -0.36 (95% CI -0.56, -0.17; I2 = 0%; fixed effects; n = 4); pectin -0.26 (95% CI -0.53, 0.02; I2 = 0%; fixed effects; n = 2); only four test products significantly reduced energy intake: 5 g alginate and 5 g guar gum in milk beverages, 9 g alginate in chocolate cookies and 25 g polydextrose in chocolate-flavoured beverages
range: 15 RCT articles (17 interventional studies; 31 soluble-fibre types, doses or viscosities), 21 fibres from 10 articles meta-analysed; n = pooled studies per fibre; risk of bias high: only four studies clearly reported randomisation and only one was double-blinded (low Jadad scores); energy intake measured 90 to 240 min after the fibre; the polydextrose upper bound is printed both -0.017 and -0.17 (either excludes zero); no certainty rating given
citation: Salleh SN, Fairus AAH, Zahary MN, Bhaskar Raj N, Mhd Jalil AM 2019, Foods 8:15; doi:10.3390/foods8010015; pmid:30621363

parameter: share of well-characterised fibre comparisons efficacious for any appetite outcome, and which fibre property predicts efficacy
value: in 51 of 90 comparisons the fibre was efficacious for >= 1 appetite-related outcome; reported differences in viscosity, molecular weight or fermentability did not clearly correspond to differences in efficacy, whereas gel-forming fibre sources were consistently efficacious (but with very few comparisons)
range: systematic search; 49 articles with 90 comparisons, acute and sustained-exposure trials; included only where the fibre's viscosity, gelling, fermentability or molecular weight was reported; the authors judge methods too inconsistent for generalised conclusions; no certainty rating given
citation: Poutanen KS, Dussort P, Erkner A et al 2017, Am J Clin Nutr 106:747-754; doi:10.3945/ajcn.117.157172; pmid:28724643

parameter: appetite and ad libitum intake under higher vs lower cereal fibre, by cereal source
value: cereal fibre associated with favourable effects on satiety and other appetite measures but limited effects on ad libitum energy intake; rye and oat fibre superior on appetite; wheat and barley fibres, and functional fibres, resistant starch and soluble corn fibre, showed a weak effect on appetite sensations and ad libitum energy intake
range: systematic review of 48 randomised crossover studies, appetite >= 2 h, washout >= 3 days; quality by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics Quality Criteria Checklist and the Health Canada Consistency Tool; no pooled estimate; PROSPERO CRD42023395182
citation: Machalias A, Ferguson JJA, Guy T, Beck EJ 2026, Nutr Rev 84:47-68; doi:10.1093/nutrit/nuaf083; pmid:40644449

parameter: satiety from an interaction of added fibre with dietary fat (acute)
value: a meta-analysis of a fat-fibre interaction on satiety found no significant effects; fat per kJ had a weak effect on satiation
range: systematic review of acute studies to December 2017; 1490 records reduced to 12 included studies; no certainty rating given
citation: Warrilow A, Mellor D, McKune A, Pumpa K 2019, Eur J Clin Nutr 73:333-344; doi:10.1038/s41430-018-0295-7; pmid:30166637

parameter: ad libitum lunch and daily energy intake after polydextrose in a mid-morning snack, and its dose-response per gram
value: lunch energy intake reduced (SMD = 0.35; P < 0.01; I2 = 0); EI at lunch (%) = -0.67 x polydextrose (g/day) (R2 = 0.80; P < 0.01); rest-of-day and daily intake not different in the meta-analysis, but EI daily (%) = -0.35 x polydextrose (g/day) (R2 = 0.68; P < 0.05)
range: 6 studies in the lunch analysis, 3 in the rest-of-day and daily analyses; PRISMA; Ibarra, Olli and Tiihonen are with DuPont Nutrition & Health (the polydextrose supplier), Alhoniemi with Avoltus Oy; no certainty rating given
population: adults; polydextrose in a mid-morning snack
citation: Ibarra A, Astbury NM, Olli K, Alhoniemi E, Tiihonen K 2015, Appetite 87:30-37; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2014.12.099; pmid:25510531

parameter: subjective appetite (VAS iAUC) after polydextrose in the satiation and satiety periods
value: desire to eat in the satiation period reduced (SMD = 0.24, I2 < 0.01, p = 0.018), in men SMD = 0.35 (p = 0.015); no other significant results across hunger, satisfaction, fullness, prospective consumption and desire to eat
range: 7 studies; Ibarra, Olli and Tiihonen are with DuPont Nutrition & Health (the polydextrose supplier), Alhoniemi with Avoltus Oy; no certainty rating given
citation: Ibarra A, Astbury NM, Olli K, Alhoniemi E, Tiihonen K 2016, Nutrients 8:45; doi:10.3390/nu8010045; pmid:26784221

parameter: appetite, energy intake and body weight under inulin-type fructan supplementation (the null reading for fructans)
value: adults: 5 RCTs found no effect on appetite sensations; 11 RCTs found no effect on daily energy intake or energy intake at a meal test; 2 of 3 RCTs on body weight showed a reduction; children: 1 RCT (n = 97, aged 9-13 y) found a reduced weight increase on 8 g/day oligofructose + inulin over 1 year
range: systematic review; adults 15 RCTs (n = 545), children 4 RCTs (n = 232); no pooled estimate; no certainty rating given
population: children and adults; well-defined inulin-type fructans vs placebo or no intervention
citation: Liber A, Szajewska H 2013, Ann Nutr Metab 63:42-54; doi:10.1159/000350312; pmid:23887189

parameter: subjective appetite after acute resistant starch, by dose and type (the pooled positive reading; S21.10 is the large-trial null)
range: 4 studies; overall I2 = 94.5% (P < 0.001); no certainty rating given
citation: Amini S, Mansoori A, Maghsumi-Norouzabad L 2021, Clin Nutr ESPEN 41:42-48; doi:10.1016/j.clnesp.2020.12.006; pmid:33487300

parameter: appetite, gut hormones and food intake after 12 weeks of 45 g/day resistant starch (RS2) vs isocaloric digestible starch (the large-trial null)
value: no effect on VAS appetite (P > 0.05), the Eating Inventory (P >= 0.24), GLP-1 (P = 0.61), PYY (P = 0.34), total (P = 0.26) or active (P = 0.47) ghrelin, buffet energy intake (P = 0.30) or free-living energy intake by remote food photography (P = 0.40)
range: randomised controlled trial; 68 enrolled, 59 analysed; secondary end points
population: adults aged 35-75 y with BMI >= 27 and prediabetes
citation: White U, Peterson CM, Beyl RA, Martin CK, Ravussin E 2020, J Acad Nutr Diet 120:1034-1041; doi:10.1016/j.jand.2020.01.017; pmid:32280055

parameter: self-reported satiety after a week of resistant-starch (RS2) wheat rolls vs wild-type wheat (a hormone change without a behavioural one)
value: fasting and peak PYY3-36 increased (q = 0.02) and GIP peak and iAUC decreased (q < 0.001), but VAS hunger or fullness did not differ after the test meal
range: double-blind randomised placebo-controlled crossover; the hormone readings exploratory; mechanism-only for satiety
citation: Hughes RL, Horn WF, Wen A et al 2022, Appetite 168:105802; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2021.105802; pmid:34774669

parameter: ad libitum lunch intake and satiety after an alginate preload at two volumes
value: low volume (9.9 g alginate in 330 ml): lunch energy intake 8.0% lower than placebo (P = 0.040) without differences in satiety feelings or paracetamol concentrations; high volume (15.0 g in 500 ml): satiety raised (P = 0.038), hunger (P = 0.042) and prospective consumption (P = 0.027) reduced, paracetamol iAUC reduced (P = 0.05), but energy intake only 5.5% lower (P = 0.20)
range: four-way placebo-controlled double-blind crossover; preloads 30 min before a fixed breakfast and again before an ad libitum lunch
citation: Georg Jensen M, Kristensen M, Belza A, Knudsen JC, Astrup A 2012, Obesity (Silver Spring) 20:1851-1858; doi:10.1038/oby.2011.232; pmid:21779093

parameter: daily energy intake over 7 days of preprandial strong-gelling sodium alginate vs control (free-living; the positive reading against S21.14's alginate null)
value: mean daily energy intake reduced by 134.8 kcal (7%), with reductions in carbohydrate, sugar, fat, saturated fat and protein; no interaction with gender, BMI class or preload timing
range: randomised controlled two-way crossover
citation: Paxman JR, Richardson JC, Dettmar PW, Corfe BM 2008, Appetite 51:713-719; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2008.06.013; pmid:18655817

parameter: gastric emptying, gastric volumes, satiation, free-choice meal intake and gut hormones after 10 days of alginate capsules vs placebo (the null reading for alginate)
value: no treatment effects on gastric emptying or volumes, ghrelin, CCK, GLP-1 or PYY, satiation, or total and macronutrient calorie intake at a free-choice meal
range: randomised 1:1 placebo-controlled allocation-concealed trial; three capsules a day 30 min before the main meal, six before testing on days 8-10
population: 48 overweight or obese adults without psychiatric comorbidity or binge eating disorder
citation: Odunsi ST, Vazquez-Roque MI, Camilleri M et al 2010, Obesity (Silver Spring) 18:1579-1584; doi:10.1038/oby.2009.421; pmid:19960001

parameter: energy intake on a twice-daily calcium-gelled alginate-pectin beverage vs control, by dietary restraint
value: food intake at dinner reduced for both the 1.0 g and 2.8 g formulations vs control; women in the lower 50th percentile of rigid restraint ate 12% less energy during the day and 22% less at the evening snack on 2.8 g; no effect in the upper 50th percentile
range: within-subjects double-blind placebo-controlled; 1-week treatment periods with 1-week washout; intake on days 1 and 7
citation: Pelkman CL, Navia JL, Miller AE, Pohle RJ 2007, Am J Clin Nutr 86:1595-1602; doi:10.1093/ajcn/86.5.1595; pmid:18065575

parameter: inter-meal hunger and fullness over 3 days of psyllium before breakfast and lunch, by dose
value: 3.4 g, 6.8 g and 10.2 g all gave directional or significant reductions in hunger and desire to eat and increased fullness between meals vs placebo, the two higher doses better than placebo or 3.4 g, and 6.8 g the most consistent (p <= 0.013); in a second study with an energy-restricted breakfast, 6.8 g reduced 3-day mean hunger and desire to eat and raised fullness (p <= 0.004)
range: two sequential randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trials; Brum and Gibb are with Procter & Gamble, maker of the psyllium product (Metamucil); no intake outcome
citation: Brum JM, Gibb RD, Peters JC, Mattes RD 2016, Appetite 105:27-36; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2016.04.041; pmid:27166077

parameter: ad libitum intake 75 min after a high insoluble-fibre cereal vs a low-fibre cereal, white bread and water (insoluble fibre)
value: ad libitum intake 937 +/- 86 kcal after the high-fibre cereal (33 g insoluble fibre), 970 +/- 65 after white bread, 1109 +/- 90 after the low-fibre cereal and 1224 +/- 89 after water (P < 0.001); appetite lower after the high-fibre cereal than white bread but not different from the low-fibre cereal
range: crossover; caloric treatments matched for energy, macronutrients, volume and weight
population: healthy young men after an overnight fast
citation: Samra RA, Anderson GH 2007, Am J Clin Nutr 86:972-979; doi:10.1093/ajcn/86.4.972; pmid:17921373

parameter: gastric-emptying half-time after 4 weeks of 20 g/day apple pectin vs alpha-cellulose (viscous vs insoluble fibre, sustained intake)
value: gastric emptying half-time prolonged approximately twofold after pectin (p < 0.005), returning to normal 3 weeks after pectin stopped; cellulose did not alter the gastric emptying rate
range: 2 wk low-fibre (3 g) diet, then 4 wk isocaloric diet with 20 g/day pectin (7 subjects) or cellulose (6 subjects); low-fibre test breakfast labelled with technetium sulfur-colloid; no appetite outcome
citation: Schwartz SE, Levine RA, Singh A, Scheidecker JR, Track NS 1982, Gastroenterology 83:812-817; doi:10.1016/s0016-5085(82)80010-3; pmid:6286402

parameter: gastric-emptying half-time and lag phase of a beta-glucan-enriched oat bread vs a whole-wheat bread at 25 g available carbohydrate
value: oat bread increased T1/2 by 18 min (p = 0.005) and Tlag by 14 min (p = 0.010); gastric emptying rate not different (p = 0.562); GLP-1 not different (p = 0.892)
range: randomised crossover; ultrasound antral area to 120 min; no appetite or intake outcome
citation: Revheim I, Ballance S, Standal AF et al 2024, Nutr Metab (Lond) 21:13; doi:10.1186/s12986-024-00789-w; pmid:38500209

parameter: gastric emptying and satiety across a 1000-fold range of meal viscosity (non-nutrient locust bean gum meals)
value: despite a 1000-fold range of initial viscosity there was only a small delay in gastric emptying (P for trend < 0.05); all meals underwent rapid intragastric dilution; satiety AUC increased and hunger AUC decreased with initial viscosity (P < 0.05)
range: 500 mL meals of 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 or 1.5 g/100 g locust bean gum; echo-planar MRI
citation: Marciani L, Gowland PA, Spiller RC et al 2000, J Nutr 130:122-127; doi:10.1093/jn/130.1.122; pmid:10613778

parameter: gastric emptying, gastric volume and fullness for meals of low or high viscosity, with or without nutrients (viscosity against nutrient load)
value: adding nutrients to the high-viscosity meal delayed gastric emptying from 46 +/- 9 to 76 +/- 6 min (P < 0.004), whereas increasing viscosity had a smaller effect; fullness linear in total gastric volume for the nutrient meals (R2 = 0.98), logarithmic for the non-nutrient meals (R2 = 0.96); fullness higher for high- than low-viscosity meals (P < 0.02)
range: four polysaccharide test meals; MRI; no intake outcome
citation: Marciani L, Gowland PA, Spiller RC et al 2001, Am J Physiol Gastrointest Liver Physiol 280:G1227-G1233; doi:10.1152/ajpgi.2001.280.6.g1227; pmid:11352816

parameter: fullness at the same gastric volume after strong- or weak-gelling alginate or guar gum (gel lumps in the stomach)
value: gastric emptying similar for all 4 meals, but fullness at the same gastric volume significantly greater for all 3 viscous meals than control; strong-gelling alginate (P = 0.031) and guar (P = 0.041) increased fullness at 115 min; strong-gelling alginate decreased hunger at 115 min (P = 0.041) and 240 min (P = 0.041)
range: 325 mL milk-based meal-replacer beverage with 1% by weight alginate or guar gum, or control; serial MRI; satiety recorded for 4 h; no intake outcome
citation: Hoad CL, Rayment P, Spiller RC et al 2004, J Nutr 134:2293-2300; doi:10.1093/jn/134.9.2293; pmid:15333719

parameter: return of hunger after guar gum in low- and high-fat soups and its relation to gastric emptying
value: 3% guar gum delayed emptying of the low-fat soup, and the small delays in the return of hunger and decline of fullness correlated with gastric emptying; with the high-fat soup the delays in return of hunger and decline of fullness were far greater and not correlated with the small additional delay in emptying
range: crossover; no intake outcome
citation: French SJ, Read NW 1994, Am J Clin Nutr 59:87-91; doi:10.1093/ajcn/59.1.87; pmid:8279409

parameter: ad libitum energy intake after colonic propionate delivery (inulin-propionate ester), and weight gain over 24 weeks
value: acute 10 g inulin-propionate ester vs inulin-control: buffet intake 300 min after a standard breakfast fell from 1175 kcal (95% CI 957 to 1392) to 1013 kcal (95% CI 816 to 1210) (p < 0.01), a mean reduction of 13.8%, with higher PYY and GLP-1 at 240-420 min and no suppression of subjective appetite; 24 weeks of 10 g/day vs inulin-control: >= 3% weight gain in 1 of 25 (4%) vs 6 of 24 (25%) (p = 0.036), >= 5% in none vs 4 of 24 (17%) (p = 0.033); weight change -1.02 kg (95% CI -2.10 to 0.04) vs 0.38 kg (95% CI -0.95 to 1.72), p = 0.099; change in ad libitum meal intake at week 24 not different between groups (p = 0.972)
range: acute randomised controlled crossover (n = 20); long-term randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel trial, 60 randomised, 49 analysed; no certainty rating given
population: acute: 20 volunteers (healthy subjects, per the discussion); long-term: overweight adults aged 40-65 y, BMI 25-40
citation: Chambers ES, Viardot A, Psichas A et al 2015, Gut 64:1744-1754; doi:10.1136/gutjnl-2014-307913; pmid:25500202

parameter: satiety and energy intake over 2 weeks of 16 g/day oligofructose vs maltodextrin (fermentable fibre, pilot)
value: satiety increased after breakfast (P = 0.04) and dinner (P = 0.04); hunger (P = 0.04) and prospective consumption (P = 0.05) reduced after dinner; energy intake lower at breakfast (P = 0.01) and lunch (P = 0.03); total daily energy intake 5% lower on oligofructose
range: single-blinded randomised placebo-controlled crossover pilot; 2-week phases, 2-week washout
population: 5 men and 5 women aged 21-39 y, BMI 18.5-27.4
citation: Cani PD, Joly E, Horsmans Y, Delzenne NM 2006, Eur J Clin Nutr 60:567-572; doi:10.1038/sj.ejcn.1602350; pmid:16340949

parameter: satiety at breakfast after an evening meal rich in indigestible carbohydrate (the second-meal effect) and its link to colonic fermentation
value: barley-kernel or fibre-and-resistant-starch-enriched evening breads improved next-morning glucose tolerance vs white wheat bread (P < 0.05); breath hydrogen correlated positively with breakfast satiety (r = 0.27; P < 0.01) and inversely with gastric emptying rate (r = -0.23; P < 0.05)
range: crossover; evening meals of 50 g available starch; no intake outcome
citation: Nilsson AC, Ostman EM, Holst JJ, Bjorck IM 2008, J Nutr 138:732-739; doi:10.1093/jn/138.4.732; pmid:18356328

parameter: hunger and appetite hormones at a standard breakfast 11-14 h after an evening meal of brown beans vs white wheat bread (the second-meal effect)
value: hunger sensations -15% (p = 0.05), PYY +51% (p < 0.001), ghrelin -14% (p < 0.05); breath H2 +141% (p < 0.01), plasma propionate +16% (p < 0.05)
range: randomised crossover; no intake outcome
citation: Nilsson A, Johansson E, Ekstrom L, Bjorck I 2013, PLoS One 8:e59985; doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0059985; pmid:23577078

parameter: satiety and second-meal intake after pulses vs isocaloric controls (acute)
value: satiety iAUC 31% greater (ratio of means 1.31, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.58, P = 0.004; I2 = 0%); second-meal intake not affected (MD -19.94, 95% CI -75 to 35, P = 0.48; I2 = 63%)
range: 9 acute controlled trials; random effects; the authors note small samples, narrow participant characteristics and unexplained heterogeneity; no certainty rating given
population: humans; beans, peas, chickpeas and lentils vs isocaloric controls
citation: Li SS, Kendall CW, de Souza RJ et al 2014, Obesity (Silver Spring) 22:1773-1780; doi:10.1002/oby.20782; pmid:24820437

parameter: subjective appetite and energy intake after whole-grain vs refined-grain foods, and its dependence on how the arms were matched (the reading that the effect follows the portion's mass)
value: hunger AUC SMD -0.34 (95% CI -0.46, -0.22), fullness 0.49 (0.31, 0.66), satiety 0.33 (0.18, 0.47), desire to eat -0.33 (-0.46, -0.20); energy intake SMD -0.11 (95% CI -0.23, 0.01; P = 0.070), significant only above the median 90.1 g whole grain; arms matched by available carbohydrate: hunger -0.44 (-0.59, -0.30), fullness 0.57 (0.37, 0.77); arms matched by calories: hunger -0.10 (-0.33, 0.14), fullness 0.19 (-0.18, 0.57), both non-significant; matched by calories and volume: hunger -0.22 (-0.47, 0.03)
range: 36 RCTs reviewed, 32 pooled; hunger I2 = 15.17%, fullness I2 = 36.76%; energy intake 29 comparisons from 17 studies, I2 = 7.44%; GRADE moderate for appetite and energy intake (low for prospective consumption), downgraded for risk of bias and possible publication bias; funded by General Mills
citation: Sanders LM, Zhu Y, Wilcox ML, Koecher K, Maki KC 2021, Adv Nutr 12:1177-1195; doi:10.1093/advances/nmaa178; pmid:33530093

parameter: lunch energy intake and fullness after apple as whole fruit, applesauce or juice (with and without added fibre), matched for weight, energy, energy density and ingestion rate
value: whole apple reduced lunch energy intake (preload + test meal) by 15% (187 +/- 36 kcal) vs no preload (p < 0.0001) and decreased intake vs applesauce and both juices; fullness apple > applesauce > both juices > control; adding naturally occurring levels of fibre to juice did not enhance satiety
range: within-subjects, once a week for 5 weeks; preloads 266 g, 125 kcal, 15 min before an ad libitum meal
citation: Flood-Obbagy JE, Rolls BJ 2009, Appetite 52:416-422; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2008.12.001; pmid:19110020

parameter: gastric-emptying half-time and fullness after isocaloric whole apple, apple puree or apple juice
value: GE t50 65 (3.3) min for whole apple vs 41 (2.8) min for puree and 38 (2.9) min for juice (P < 0.0001; puree and juice not different); fullness and satiety AUC 0-270 min greater for whole apple than juice (P = 0.002 and 0.004)
range: open-label 3-way randomised crossover; 178 kcal portions; MRI to 270 min; mean (SEM); no intake outcome
citation: Krishnasamy S, Lomer MCE, Marciani L et al 2020, J Nutr 150:2890-2899; doi:10.1093/jn/nxaa191; pmid:32805050

parameter: ingestion rate and satiety of apples as intact fruit, puree or fibre-free juice (fibre removal and disruption)
value: juice consumed eleven times faster than intact apples and four times faster than puree; with ingestion rate equalised, juice significantly less satisfying than puree, and puree than apples
range: test meals of 60 g available carbohydrate; satiety scored numerically; no intake outcome

population: children aged 7.6 y (n = 422), followed at 9.8 y (n = 387) and 15.8 y (n = 229), Finland
citation: Saner C, Senior AM, Zhang H, Eloranta AM, Magnussen CG, Sabin MA et al 2023, Eur J Clin Nutr 77:652-659; doi:10.1038/s41430-023-01276-w; pmid:36797489

parameter: protein balance against energy intake in pregnancy (the null reading of protein leverage, against the population L estimates)
value: protein balance in early pregnancy not significantly associated with energy intake across mid and mid/late pregnancy (beta = 328.7, p = 0.30; beta = 286.2, p = 0.26) or gestational weight gain (beta = 117.0, p = 0.41)
range: energy intake by the intake-balance method; protein by food photography as a ratio of the pregnancy EAR (0.88 g/kg/d); small cohort
population: 41 pregnant women with obesity, pregravid BMI 34.4 (2.9) kg/m2
citation: Kebbe M, Most J, Altazan AD, Redman LM 2023, Obesity (Silver Spring) 31:2057-2064; doi:10.1002/oby.23789; pmid:37387452

parameter: whether a negative association of energy intake with percent protein in survey data can arise without protein leverage (the method caveat on the L estimates)
value: patterns consistent with protein leverage do not emerge simply because protein intake has a lower mean and/or variance than non-protein intake; they are observed where protein has a lower index of dispersion (variance/mean) than non-protein intake; disentangling causality is beyond the power of observational data alone
range: analytical models validated by simulation; cited for the shape of the inference, not for an effect size
citation: Senior AM, Raubenheimer D, Simpson SJ 2022, R Soc Open Sci 9:220756; doi:10.1098/rsos.220756; pmid:36177194

parameter: protein intake on an ultra-processed vs an unprocessed diet matched for presented macronutrients, eaten ad libitum (protein intake held while energy rose)
value: energy intake greater on the ultra-processed diet by 508 +/- 106 kcal/d (p = 0.0001), from carbohydrate (280 +/- 54 kcal/d) and fat (230 +/- 53 kcal/d) but not protein (-2 +/- 12 kcal/d; p = 0.85); weight +0.9 +/- 0.3 kg vs -0.9 +/- 0.3 kg
range: inpatient randomised crossover, 2 weeks per diet; meals matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre; the trial does not manipulate protein share, so it is consistent with but not a test of leverage
citation: Hall KD, Ayuketah A, Brychta R, Cai H, Cassimatis T, Chen KY et al 2019, Cell Metab 30:67-77.e3; doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008; pmid:31105044

parameter: ad libitum energy intake and expenditure on a high-protein (30 %) vs a normal-protein (13 %) ultra-processed diet over 54 h
value: energy intake -196 +/- 396 kcal/d and energy expenditure +128 +/- 98 kcal/d on the high-protein diet; energy balance less positive (18% vs 32%); postprandial ghrelin lower, glucagon and PYY higher
range: single-blind randomised crossover in a whole-room calorimeter; meals equally palatable, matched for calories, fat and fibre; carbohydrate 29% vs 46%
citation: Hagele FA, Herpich C, Koop J, Grubbel J, Dorner R, Fedde S et al 2025, Nat Metab 7:704-713; doi:10.1038/s42255-025-01247-4; pmid:40082711

parameter: per-meal protein dose threshold for satiety in grams (the 25-30 g per meal idea), from a pooled dose-response of ad libitum intake or time to the next meal
range: named by Satiety research 2 Task 22; no pooled source states a threshold; Kohanmoo 2020 (S1222) found appetite ratings moved at doses < 35 g, and Bertenshaw 2009 a graded intake response across 13-50% protein in a beverage; the 25-30 g figure traces to narrative reviews

parameter: pooled randomised estimate of the change in ad libitum energy intake per percentage point of dietary protein energy below the protein target, with its CI (the protein leverage gain in humans)
range: named by Satiety research 2 Task 22; the randomised trials disagree (Gosby 2011 +12% at 10 vs 15%; Martens 2013 and 2014 no rise at 5%); the population L of -0.18 to -0.37 is observational and its causal reading contested (Senior 2022)

parameter: fat vs carbohydrate per kcal, acute: appetite after an added 1.52 MJ fat or carbohydrate breakfast supplement, and energy eaten ad libitum from high-fat vs high-carbohydrate foods (the fat paradox: fat satiates weakly)
value: a 1.52 MJ (362 kcal) carbohydrate supplement at breakfast suppressed appetite 90 min later but had no effect on a test meal given after 270 min; a 1.52 MJ fat supplement produced no detectable action on measures of appetite at any time point; obese subjects eating from a range of high-fat or high-carbohydrate foods voluntarily consumed twice as much energy from the fat items, and that large fat intake exerted a disproportionately weak effect on satiety
range: three separate preload experiments plus one ad libitum study; subject numbers not given in the abstract; no certainty rating given; a symposium paper reporting the group's experiments
population: lean adults (preload experiments); obese adults (ad libitum food-range study)
citation: Blundell JE, Burley VJ, Cotton JR, Lawton CL 1993, Am J Clin Nutr 57(5 Suppl):772S-777S; doi:10.1093/ajcn/57.5.772s; pmid:8475895
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: spontaneous daily energy intake over 2 weeks on covertly manipulated low-, medium- and high-fat diets of similar appearance and palatability (passive overconsumption of fat, chronic)
value: relative to the medium-fat diet (30-35% of energy from fat), subjects spontaneously consumed an 11.3% deficit on the low-fat diet (15-20%) and a 15.4% surfeit on the high-fat diet (45-50%) (p < 0.0001), with significant body-weight changes (p < 0.001); a small amount of caloric compensation did occur (p < 0.02), greatest in the leanest subjects (p < 0.03)
range: n = 24, each through a sequence of three 2-wk treatments; no certainty rating given; energy density rose with fat, so fat and energy density are not separated
citation: Lissner L, Levitsky DA, Strupp BJ, Kalkwarf HJ, Roe DA 1987, Am J Clin Nutr 46:886-892; doi:10.1093/ajcn/46.6.886; pmid:3687822

parameter: energy balance over 7 days in a calorimeter on covertly manipulated low-, medium- and high-fat diets eaten ad libitum (fat has no apparent reductive effect on next-day intake)
value: diets 20/40/60% of energy as fat at 4.80, 5.59 and 7.04 kJ/g; energy intake rose with percent fat (P < 0.001), giving average daily balances of -0.27, 0.77 and 2.58 MJ/d on the low-, medium- and high-fat diets; carbohydrate balance related negatively to the next day's energy balance (P = 0.0082, 5.5% of variance) and fat balance positively (P < 0.0001, 19.9% of variance); the authors find a potential for protein and carbohydrate to reduce subsequent intake and no apparent reductive effect of fat
range: n = 6, three 7-d occasions each; no certainty rating given; fat and energy density co-varied by design
population: lean men confined to a whole-body indirect calorimeter
citation: Stubbs RJ, Harbron CG, Murgatroyd PR, Prentice AM 1995, Am J Clin Nutr 62:316-329; doi:10.1093/ajcn/62.2.316; pmid:7625338

parameter: energy intake and expenditure over 2 weeks per diet on covertly manipulated low-, medium- and high-fat diets eaten ad libitum while free-living
value: energy intakes 9.11, 10.32 and 12.78 MJ/d on the low- (20% fat), medium- (40%) and high-fat (60%) diets, almost identical to the calorimeter study (9.02, 10.2 and 12.35 MJ/d); doubly labelled water expenditure 12.45, 12.10 and 11.97 MJ/d

population: men resident in but not confined to a metabolic suite
citation: Stubbs RJ, Ritz P, Coward WA, Prentice AM 1995, Am J Clin Nutr 62:330-337; doi:10.1093/ajcn/62.2.330; pmid:7625339
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: body weight after at least 6 months on a lower vs higher total-fat diet without any intention to lose weight (pooled; the chronic fat effect is small)
value: mean body weight reduction of 1.4 kg (95% CI -1.7 to -1.1 kg) on lower fat; BMI -0.5 kg/m2 (95% CI -0.6 to -0.3); greater fat reduction, lower baseline fat intake and higher baseline BMI associated with greater weight reduction; the effect does not alter over time
range: 26 RCTs, 53,875 participants for weight (37 RCTs, 57,079 participants in all); I2 = 75%, explained by subgrouping and meta-regression; GRADE high-consistency evidence, not downgraded
population: adults not aiming to lose weight, trials of 6 months or longer
citation: Hooper L, Abdelhamid AS, Jimoh OF, Bunn D, Skeaff CM 2020, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 6:CD013636; doi:10.1002/14651858.CD013636; pmid:32476140

parameter: ad libitum energy intake on a minimally processed plant-based low-fat high-carbohydrate diet vs an animal-based ketogenic low-carbohydrate diet (the reading that a very high fat share does not lower intake, against the carbohydrate-insulin model)
value: the low-fat diet (10.3% fat, 75.2% carbohydrate, glycaemic load 85 g/1,000 kcal) led to 689 +/- 73 kcal/d less energy intake than the low-carbohydrate diet (75.8% fat, 10.0% carbohydrate, 6 g/1,000 kcal) over 2 weeks (P < 0.0001) and 544 +/- 68 kcal/d less over the final week (P < 0.0001)

population: adults aged 29.9 +/- 1.4 y, BMI 27.8 +/- 1.3 kg/m2, inpatients at the NIH Clinical Center
citation: Hall KD, Guo J, Courville AB et al 2021, Nat Med 27:344-353; doi:10.1038/s41591-020-01209-1; pmid:33479499
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: energy intake at the next meal after a low- vs high-glycaemic-index breakfast (pooled; the reading that breakfast GI has no effect)
value: no effect of breakfast GI on subsequent short-term energy intake: ES = -0.01, 95% CI (-0.21, 0.18), z = -0.12, p = 0.90
range: 9 studies, 11 trials, 183 participants; Q(10) = 18.70, p = 0.04, I2 = 46%, random effects; only one trial classified as high methodological quality
population: healthy people, randomised controlled and crossover trials
citation: Sun FH, Li C, Zhang YJ, Wong SH, Wang L 2016, Nutrients 8:37; doi:10.3390/nu8010037; pmid:26742058

value: evidence from the short-term (1 day) studies that low-glycaemic foods or meals have a higher satietogenic effect than high-glycaemic foods or meals; in the long-term studies confounding variables make it impossible to conclude that low-glycaemic diets benefit body-weight regulation; in some studies the effect of lower glycaemia cannot be separated from that of fibre
range: systematic review without pooling, 32 human intervention studies selected for control of confounders; no certainty rating given; industry-affiliated authors
population: human intervention studies (participant characteristics not given in the abstract)

parameter: body weight on low-glycaemic-index diets vs other diets (pooled, chronic)
value: small but significant improvements in body weight and BMI overall, with no individual control diet significantly different; in people with normal blood glucose who achieved a GI difference of 20 points or more, body weight SMD = -0.26 (95% CI -0.43 to -0.09)

population: adults in randomised controlled trials, normal and impaired glucose control
citation: Zafar MI, Mills KE, Zheng J, Peng MM, Ye X, Chen LL 2019, Obes Rev 20:290-315; doi:10.1111/obr.12791; pmid:30460737

population: overweight men and women, BMI about 28 kg/m2
citation: Raben A, Vasilaras TH, Moller AC, Astrup A 2002, Am J Clin Nutr 76:721-729; doi:10.1093/ajcn/76.4.721; pmid:12324283

value: at week 10 the sucrose group had a 3.3 MJ higher energy intake but felt less full and had higher ratings of prospective food consumption than the sweetener group; supplements 2 g/kg body weight, 80% beverages and 20% solid foods by weight
range: subgroup of the Raben 2002 trial, n = 12 sucrose vs 10 sweetener, single-blind; no certainty rating given
citation: Sorensen LB, Vasilaras TH, Astrup A, Raben A 2014, Am J Clin Nutr 100:36-45; doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.081554; pmid:24787495
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: dietary compensation over 4 weeks for 1800 kJ/d of sucrose drinks vs artificially sweetened drinks (the reading that liquid sugar is partly compensated, against DiMeglio and Mattes 2000)
value: sucrose drinks (4 x 250 ml/d, 1800 kJ/d) vs sweetener drinks (67 kJ/d): by 4 weeks sucrose supplements significantly reduced total carbohydrate, fat and protein intake compared with sweetener supplements (all P < 0.001); mean daily energy intake increased by just under 1000 kJ compared with baseline (P < 0.001), with a non-significant trend to weight gain in those receiving sucrose; no effects on appetite or mood; the expectancy labelling had no effect

range: two repeated-measures experiments, n = 12 and n = 19; no certainty rating given

source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: buffet intake 38 min after a 500 mL fructose vs glucose preload (the reading that fructose sates more, against Akhavan 2007 and Luo 2015)
value: after the fructose preload subjects ate fewer overall calories and fewer grams of fat than after the glucose, aspartame or plain-water preloads; aspartame did not stimulate intake beyond water
range: within-subjects design, preloads in randomised order at weekly intervals; subject numbers and magnitudes not given in the abstract; no certainty rating given

parameter: hunger, desire for food and food-reward choices after a fructose vs glucose drink
value: fructose relative to glucose led to greater hunger and desire for food, and a greater willingness to give up long-term monetary rewards to obtain immediate high-calorie foods, with smaller increases in plasma insulin
range: n = 24, double-blind random-order crossover; magnitudes not given in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Luo S, Monterosso JR, Sarpelleh K, Page KA 2015, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 112:6509-6514; doi:10.1073/pnas.1503358112; pmid:25941364
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: body weight when sugar-sweetened beverages are added (adult RCTs) and per daily serving (cohorts) (pooled)
value: RCTs in adults: body weight increased when SSBs were added, 0.85 kg (95% CI 0.50, 1.20 kg; random and fixed effects); cohorts in adults: 0.22 kg (95% CI 0.09, 0.34) random and 0.12 kg (0.10, 0.14) fixed per daily serving over 1 y; RCTs in children: BMI gain -0.17 (95% CI -0.39, 0.05) random when SSBs were reduced

value: weight increased by 7.37 kg in the sugar group vs 6.35 kg in the sugar-free group (95% CI of the difference -1.54 to -0.48 kg); BMI z score +0.15 vs +0.02 SD units (95% CI of the difference -0.21 to -0.05); skinfolds, waist-to-height ratio and fat mass also rose less on sugar-free
range: n = 641, double-blind, 18 mo; 26% stopped drinking, data imputed; completers-plus-discontinued analysis BMI z +0.12 vs +0.06 (P = 0.06); no certainty rating given

citation: de Ruyter JC, Olthof MR, Seidell JC, Katan MB 2012, N Engl J Med 367:1397-1406; doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1203034; pmid:22998340
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/23-carbohydrate-and-fat.md § Satiety research 2, carbohydrate and fat harvest (2026-10-09)

value: energy intake control 4,604 +/- 464 kJ, C10 4,109 +/- 588 kJ, C12 1,747 +/- 632 kJ (P < 0.001, C12 vs control and C10); C12 but not C10 suppressed appetite perceptions and induced nausea; C12 raised CCK far more than C10 and stimulated GLP-1

value: canola and peanut oil muffins gave higher fullness, and all three fat muffins lower hunger at 30, 60 and 120 min, than the fat-free muffin; no differences among the fat-containing loads, including 24-h intake; intake after the session was higher after the fat-free muffin, but total intake including the preload was similar across treatments
