citation: Flanagan EW, Sanchez-Delgado G, Martin CK et al 2024, iScience 27:109842; doi:10.1016/j.isci.2024.109842; pmid:38947494
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: compensatory decline in non-exercise physical activity or thermogenesis under diet and exercise interventions
value: compensation observed in 26 of 70 intervention arms (15 of 36 studies reporting declines in NEAT, NEPA or both): 63%, 27% and 23% of diet-only, combined diet and exercise, and exercise-only arms; weight loss in participants who decreased NEAT double that of non-compensators
range: 36 articles (10 RCT, 9 randomised, 17 non-randomised trials), 70 arms, 1561 participants, interventions >= 7 days; objective activity measures; the authors note underpowered designs; no pooled estimate and no certainty rating given
citation: Silva AM, Judice PB, Carraca EV et al 2018, Br J Nutr 119:1327-1345; doi:10.1017/S000711451800096X; pmid:29845903
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: whether increased exercise or physical activity changes ad libitum daily energy intake (systematic review by design)
value: no effect of activity, exercise or training on energy intake in 59% of cross-sectional (n = 17), 69% of acute (n = 40), 50% of short-term (n = 10), 92% of non-randomised (n = 12) and 75% of randomised trials (n = 24); no consistent evidence that increased physical activity or exercise affects energy or macronutrient intake
range: 99 articles (103 studies), 1990-2013; meta-analysis judged inappropriate for heterogeneity, so vote counting by design; the authors name a lack of adequately powered trials of sufficient duration; no certainty rating given
citation: Donnelly JE, Herrmann SD, Lambourne K et al 2014, PLoS One 9:e83498; doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0083498; pmid:24454704
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: body-weight change during 3 to 34 days of military training or deployment on combat rations
value: mean body weight reductions from a negligible 0.1% (8 days of combat training) to approximately 8.3% (12 days of energy restriction in a US Army Ranger course), with decreases in fat mass, fat-free mass and percentage body fat; energy intake from combat rations often falls short of requirements
range: systematic review of 30 studies (3-34 days), ten databases to October 2016; narrative synthesis; quality by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics checklist, many studies at risk of bias; no pooled estimate
population: military personnel in training or deployment
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: energy balance by training event across a 64-day special forces field phase (intake keeps up with moderate field work but not with strenuous)
value: simulated urban combat elicited the largest energy deficit, 11.3 +/- 2.3 MJ/day (2700 +/- 550 kcal/day), and body-mass reduction (3.3 +/- 1.9 kg); energy balance maintained during weapons familiarisation and platoon-size raids; over the course body mass -4.2 +/- 3.7 kg, fat mass -2.8 +/- 2.0 kg, fat-free mass -1.4 +/- 2.8 kg
range: four groups measured over 10-day periods; expenditure by doubly labelled water; intake from distributed minus uneaten rations or dining facility; no certainty rating given
population: 36 male soldiers (28 +/- 5 y, 83 +/- 7 kg) in the Special Forces Qualification Course
citation: Margolis LM, Rood J, Champagne C, Young AJ, Castellani JW 2013, Appl Physiol Nutr Metab 38:396-400; doi:10.1139/apnm-2012-0323; pmid:23713532
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: appetite and 24-h ad libitum ration intake during 8 h with two 2-h circuits of military tasks at 30, 21 and -10 C vs sedentary (the reading of no intake change with heat, cold or work, against Millet 2021's pooled cold rise and heat fall, S1316)
value: appetite perceived as suppressed in the heat compared with the cold (p < 0.05); dietary intake not different between conditions (p > 0.05); relative intake (24-h intake minus 24-h expenditure) higher in the sedentary condition than in any active condition (p < 0.05); 83% of participants in positive balance when sedentary and most (80%) of the active conditions in negative balance; acylated ghrelin Sedentary = Cold > Temperate = Hot
range: randomised repeated measures, four 8-h trials in a thermal chamber; field rations ad libitum; no certainty rating given
population: 18 Canadian Armed Forces members (14 men, 4 women)
citation: Mandic I, Ahmed M, Rhind S et al 2019, Nutr Metab (Lond) 16:29; doi:10.1186/s12986-019-0348-5; pmid:31080490
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: ad libitum breakfast intake after a fasted 40-min run in heat (36 C) vs neutral (25 C) vs rest
value: intake greater after exercise in the neutral temperature than control (P = 0.021) but similar between exercise in the heat and control and between the two exercise trials; relative intake after exercise in the heat lower than control (P = 0.002); the lower relative intake associated with raised tympanic temperature and PYY
range: randomised counterbalanced crossover, three trials; running at 70% VO2peak; intake magnitudes not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Shorten AL, Wallman KE, Guelfi KJ 2009, Am J Clin Nutr 90:1215-1221; doi:10.3945/ajcn.2009.28162; pmid:19793848
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: ad libitum intake 45 min after a 45-min brisk walk in cold air (8 C) vs neutral air (20 C)
value: intake 1299 +/- 657 kcal after exercise in the cold vs 1172 +/- 537 kcal in the neutral environment (P < 0.05); the change in acylated ghrelin and its AUC greater during walking in the cold (P < 0.05)
range: randomised counterbalanced crossover; covert buffet measurement; no certainty rating given
population: 16 overweight adults (10 men, 6 women; 50.1 +/- 11.6 y; BMI 28.9 +/- 4.2 kg/m2)
citation: Crabtree DR, Blannin AK 2015, Med Sci Sports Exerc 47:49-57; doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000391; pmid:24870575
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: hunger and energy intake in hypoxia (altitude) vs normoxia (pooled)
value: postprandial hunger SMD -0.15 (95% CI -0.29 to -0.01; 14 comparisons; p = 0.043), trivial; energy intake SMD -0.50 (95% CI -0.85 to -0.15; 8 comparisons; p = 0.006), moderate; postprandial acylated ghrelin SMD -0.16 (95% CI -0.25 to -0.08); fasted insulin SMD 0.41 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.65); ghrelin fell and insulin rose further with hypoxic severity (meta-regression p = 0.010 and p = 0.020)
range: 28 within-measures studies (54 fasted and 22 postprandial comparisons), searched to April 2017; random effects; no GRADE rating given
population: adults exposed to real or simulated altitude, at rest or with exercise
citation: Matu J, Gonzalez JT, Ispoglou T, Duckworth L, Deighton K 2018, Appetite 125:98-108; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2018.01.015; pmid:29374575
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: the effect of load carriage (pack weight) on hunger and intake at a matched energy expenditure
range: no controlled reading found on 2026-10-09; the expenditure side is carried by the energy report's Pandolf load-carriage terms and the field compilation of Tharion 2005 (S1324), the appetite side only by trials of unloaded running, cycling, walking and resistance work
population: people carrying loads during work or travel
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: the sex difference, if any, in intake compensation for weeks of added exercise at a matched dose
range: readings disagree: approximately 33% compensation in women and none in men over 7 days (Stubbs 2002, two papers); a rise in men (P = 0.031) and not women (P = 0.118) over 14 days (Whybrow 2008, S1318); higher intake in nonresponders only among men over 10 months (Herrmann 2015); a larger ghrelin rise in women (Hagobian 2009); no sex difference in the narrative consensus (Thackray 2016) or in compensators (Flanagan 2024); no pooled sex contrast
population: men and women under weeks of added exercise, feeding ad libitum
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: the effect of hot or cold surroundings on intake over days of outdoor work, beyond the first 24 h
range: acute readings only: the pooled cold rise and heat fall within a day (Millet 2021, S1316), no intake change within 24 h of work in heat or cold (Mandic 2019), the cold-water and cold-air rises (White 2005, Crabtree 2015, Grigg 2023 S1315); the multi-day cold expeditions (Charlot 2020, 2021, S1326-S1327) have no thermoneutral control
population: people working outdoors in heat or cold for days
source: docs/superpowers/research/2026-10-09-satiety-research-2/25-exercise.md § Satiety research 2, exercise and appetite, extended harvest (2026-10-09)

parameter: total and non-breast-milk energy intake on days of diarrhoea or fever vs symptom-free days (acute, during the illness)
value: total energy intake fell 5-6% during diarrhoea or fever; energy from non-breast-milk foods fell 20-30%; breast-milk intake, feeding frequency and suckling time did not change; symptom-free intake 557 +/- 128 kcal/d (infants under 181 d) and 638 +/- 193 kcal/d (over 180 d)
range: 1615 full-day observations, models controlling for age, season and individual; no certainty rating given
population: 131 infants, Huascar (Lima), Peru, community-based longitudinal surveillance
citation: Brown KH, Stallings RY, de Kanashiro HC, Lopez de Romaña G, Black RE 1990, Am J Clin Nutr 52:1005-1013; doi:10.1093/ajcn/52.6.1005; pmid:2239775

parameter: share of hospitalised patients who eat less than the meal served, and 30-day mortality by the fraction eaten
value: more than half of the patients did not eat their full hospital meal; adjusted hazard ratio for death in hospital within 30 days 2.10 (1.53-2.89) when eating about a quarter of the meal and 3.02 (2.11-4.32) when eating nothing
range: one-day multinational cross-sectional survey with competing-risk analysis; illness type not separated; no certainty rating given
population: 16,290 adult hospitalised patients, European hospitals, 19 January 2006
citation: Hiesmayr M, Schindler K, Pernicka E et al 2009, Clin Nutr 28:484-491; doi:10.1016/j.clnu.2009.05.013; pmid:19573957

parameter: mechanism of the anorexia of infection (mechanism only, no intake magnitude)
value: part of the acute-phase response: microbial products (lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan, bacterial DNA, viral double-stranded RNA) stimulate proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1beta, TNF-alpha, IL-6, interferons) that reduce food intake through peripheral afferents, leptin and direct action on the brain, with serotonin, dopamine, histamine, CRF, NPY and alpha-MSH as central mediators; beneficial at first, long-lasting anorexia delays recovery
range: narrative review; no certainty rating given

parameter: duration of endotoxin-induced physical sickness symptoms, a composite scale that includes reduced appetite (acute; not an appetite measure alone)
value: after 0.8 ng/kg endotoxin, bodily and psychological sickness symptoms occurred only in the acute phase; none persisted or recurred 24-72 h after injection, while serum CRP peaked at 24 h and fell until 72 h
range: randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover, 7 days apart; physical symptoms on the GASE composite; no certainty rating given
citation: Engler H, Brinkhoff A, Wilde B et al 2023, Neuroimmunomodulation 30:268-276; doi:10.1159/000534444; pmid:37797587

parameter: size (VAS mm or kcal/day) and duration of appetite loss in adults during a common acute infection or fever
range: the infant community study (Brown 1990) and the hospital survey (Hiesmayr 2009) give intake falls without hunger ratings; the human endotoxin model reports a composite symptom score only; no adult trial or cohort of hunger or ad libitum intake through a common acute infection was found

parameter: rise in resting energy expenditure per degree Celsius of fever in adults
range: no record resolved in this pass; the commonly quoted 10-13% per degree is not a resolved row

parameter: gastric emptying of a drink taken immediately after rotation-induced motion sickness (acute)
value: 47% of the isotope count remained in the stomach 1 h after ingestion following motion sickness short of vomiting, against 14% under scopolamine 0.6 mg with d-amphetamine 5 mg; neostigmine added to the drugs returned emptying to the placebo range
range: gamma-camera emptying of ten ounces of isotonic saline; sample size not given in the abstract; no certainty rating given
population: subjects in a rotating chair making head movements
citation: Wood MJ, Wood CD, Manno JE, Manno BR, Redetzki HM 1987, Aviat Space Environ Med 58:1112-1114; pmid:3318799

parameter: oral-caecal transit and normal 3-cpm gastric activity under vection-induced motion sickness, susceptible vs non-susceptible (acute)
value: oral-caecal transit 144 min in the susceptible vs 107 min in the non-susceptible group (P < 0.01); 3-cpm activity fell 8.9% from baseline to recovery in the susceptible vs 4.2%; symptom reports correlated with transit time (r = 0.43)
range: lactulose breath hydrogen and electrogastrography; no certainty rating given
population: 45 subjects in a rotating optokinetic drum
citation: Muth ER, Stern RM, Koch KL 1996, Dig Dis Sci 41:330-334; doi:10.1007/bf02093824; pmid:8601378

parameter: effect of nausea or motion sickness on hunger ratings and ad libitum food intake in healthy adults
range: nausea's effect is read only through gastric stasis and slowed transit (Wood 1987, Muth 1996); no measurement of hunger or intake under nausea in healthy adults was found

parameter: resting energy expenditure after severe burn injury, as percent of Harris-Benedict predicted, and its time course
value: 130-140% of predicted; rose immediately postburn, peaked at 2 weeks and remained elevated at discharge; lean body mass -4.1 +/- 1.9% over the acute stay
range: prospective single-centre study, weekly indirect calorimetry (n = 212); no certainty rating given
population: 242 severely burned children (> 30% total body surface area, mean 56%), mean age 8 y, no anabolic drugs
citation: Jeschke MG, Chinkes DL, Finnerty CC et al 2008, Ann Surg 248:387-401; doi:10.1097/sla.0b013e3181856241; pmid:18791359

parameter: appetite over the first 7 days after abdominal surgery
value: appetite score highest on the preoperative day and declining through the 7 postoperative days; lower in women, after general anaesthesia and after open surgery; most patients had moderate to good appetite both before and 7 days after the operation
range: Council on Nutrition Appetite Questionnaire, GEE analysis; no certainty rating given
population: 169 abdominal postoperative patients, Hanoi Medical University Hospital
citation: Nguyen TH, Ta NT, Dang AK et al 2023, Front Nutr 10:1008636; doi:10.3389/fnut.2023.1008636; pmid:37032772

parameter: effect of acute pain or a non-burn injury on hunger and ad libitum intake in otherwise healthy adults, and whether intake rises to meet injury hypermetabolism
range: the burn and surgical readings are hospital patients under clinical feeding (Jeschke 2008, Nguyen 2023); no controlled human reading of pain on hunger or intake was found

parameter: association of stress with food intake overall and by food type (pooled)
value: Hedges' g 0.114 (95% CI 0.061, 0.166) for overall food intake; unhealthy foods 0.116 (0.055, 0.177); healthy foods -0.111 (-0.165, -0.056)
range: 54 studies, combined N 119,820; I2 93.556% overall; 30 studies rated weak, 19 moderate and 5 strong quality (EPHPP)
population: healthy adults, naturalistic and laboratory stress
citation: Hill D, Conner M, Clancy F, Moss R, Wilding S, Bristow M, O'Connor DB 2022, Health Psychol Rev 16:280-304; doi:10.1080/17437199.2021.1923406; pmid:33913377

parameter: stress-food intake association by stress measure (laboratory-induced vs perceived) and by study quality (pooled; the reading that the strongest studies find almost no effect)
range: subgroup values read from the authors' accepted manuscript on OSF (HPR_ACCEPTED.pdf; Table 1 and Results), whose overall g 0.114 matches the published abstract; study quality did not moderate overall, Q(2) = 5.990, p = .050, and no pairwise quality contrast was significant (strong vs weak Q(1) = 3.183, p = .074; strong vs moderate Q(1) = 3.449, p = .063); strong-quality I2 <1%
citation: Hill D, Conner M, Clancy F, Moss R, Wilding S, Bristow M, O'Connor DB 2022, Health Psychol Rev 16:280-304; doi:10.1080/17437199.2021.1923406; pmid:33913377; doi:10.31234/osf.io/fjqsd

parameter: self-reported direction of change in the amount eaten under stress (the reading that stress lowers intake in as many people as it raises it)
value: 42% reported eating less and 38% eating more when stressed; 73% reported more snacking; dieters were more likely to report stress hyperphagia and non-dieters stress hypophagia
range: brief questionnaire; no certainty rating given

parameter: ad libitum meal intake after preparing a speech (acute social stressor) vs listening to neutral text (the null reading for total intake)
value: stress did not alter overall intake, nor intake of or appetite for six food categories; stressed emotional eaters ate more sweet high-fat food and a more energy-dense meal
range: two groups, stressor confirmed by blood pressure and mood; no certainty rating given
citation: Oliver G, Wardle J, Gibson EL 2000, Psychosom Med 62:853-865; doi:10.1097/00006842-200011000-00016; pmid:11139006

parameter: energy eaten in the absence of hunger after an acute stress task vs a control task
value: total 965.2 kJ vs 793.8 kJ (P < 0.01); from sweet foods 708.1 kJ vs 599.4 kJ (P < 0.03); the difference rose with the rise in state anxiety (R2 = 0.05), more steeply in high-disinhibition eaters (R2 = 0.12)
range: randomised crossover; no certainty rating given
population: 129 normal-weight and overweight men and women, BMI 24.5 +/- 3.4, age 27.6 +/- 8.8 y
citation: Rutters F, Nieuwenhuizen AG, Lemmens SG, Born JM, Westerterp-Plantenga MS 2009, Obesity (Silver Spring) 17:72-77; doi:10.1038/oby.2008.493; pmid:18997672

parameter: energy intake after laboratory stress in high vs low cortisol reactors
value: high cortisol reactors ate more calories than low reactors on the stress day and similar amounts on the control day; a greater rise in negative mood was related to greater intake
range: stress and control sessions on different days, within subject; high and low cortisol reactors are an observed split, not assigned; session order not stated in the abstract; amounts not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Epel E, Lapidus R, McEwen B, Brownell K 2001, Psychoneuroendocrinology 26:37-49; doi:10.1016/s0306-4530(00)00035-4; pmid:11070333

parameter: laboratory and same-evening energy intake after a Trier Social Stress Test (original or modified) vs no stress
value: intake during the laboratory visit was not affected by either stressor; evening intake was higher after the original test; cortisol reactivity did not correlate with intake
range: randomised, three arms; no certainty rating given
citation: Ghadeer TH, Redding CA, Campanella BL et al 2025, Psychoneuroendocrinology 182:107649; doi:10.1016/j.psyneuen.2025.107649; pmid:41108941

parameter: energy intake within 2 weeks of academic examinations vs a control period (chronic naturalistic stress)
value: no general effect of exam stress on food intake; total energy intake rose in students with high trait anxiety and low social support and fell in those with low trait anxiety and high social support
range: exam and control groups assessed at baseline and at exams, diet by interview; no certainty rating given
citation: Pollard TM, Steptoe A, Canaan L, Davies GJ, Wardle J 1995, Int J Behav Med 2:299-320; doi:10.1207/s15327558ijbm0204_2; pmid:16250770

parameter: eating after experimentally induced negative or positive emotion (pooled) (the reading that negative emotion raises intake only in restrained eaters, against Cardi 2015)
value: negative emotions increased eating in restrained eaters and did not affect eating in overweight or obese people, people with eating disorders or self-assessed emotional eaters; positive emotion increased eating across groups
range: 56 experimental studies, 3670 participants, random effects; heterogeneity high; pooled effect sizes not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Evers C, Dingemans A, Junghans AF, Boevé A 2018, Neurosci Biobehav Rev 92:195-208; doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2018.05.028; pmid:29860103

parameter: meal intake after induced negative or positive mood vs neutral mood (pooled) (the reading that negative mood raises intake generally, against Evers 2018)
value: induced negative mood was significantly associated with greater food intake, especially in restrained and binge eaters; positive mood was also associated with greater caloric intake across groups; the authors call the effect across a single meal small when proposing positive-mood strategies for anorexia and bulimia nervosa
range: 33 laboratory studies, 2491 participants; pooled effect sizes not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
population: healthy participants and patients with eating and weight disorders
citation: Cardi V, Leppanen J, Treasure J 2015, Neurosci Biobehav Rev 57:299-309; doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2015.08.011; pmid:26299807

parameter: chocolate intake during 1 h of induced boredom vs 1 h of a neutral documentary (acute)
value: participants ate more M&Ms when bored; in a parallel experiment they also self-administered more electric shocks when bored, read as a drive to escape monotony rather than to seek reward
range: two sessions in balanced order per experiment; amounts not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Havermans RC, Vancleef L, Kalamatianos A, Nederkoorn C 2015, Appetite 85:52-57; doi:10.1016/j.appet.2014.11.007; pmid:25447018

parameter: state boredom and food intake in a week-long diary and in two boredom-induction experiments
value: in the diary, state boredom positively predicted calorie, fat, carbohydrate and protein consumption; a high- against low-boredom task raised the self-reported desire to snack rather than eat something healthy among people high in objective self-awareness; in the consumption experiment, a boring film raised intake of less healthy and of exciting healthy foods against a sad film (not a neutral or low-boredom film) among people high in objective self-awareness
range: three studies (diary and two experiments); amounts not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
population: 33 adults in a 7-day diary (Limerick), 79 students (Study 2) and 44 students (Study 3), University of Limerick
citation: Moynihan AB, van Tilburg WA, Igou ER, Wisman A, Donnelly AE, Mulcaire JB 2015, Front Psychol 6:369; doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00369; pmid:25883579

parameter: daily energy intake and expenditure under partial sleep deprivation vs control (pooled)
value: energy intake +385 kcal (95% CI 252, 517; P < 0.00001); no significant change in total energy expenditure or resting metabolic rate; higher fat and lower protein intake
range: 17 studies (n = 496) reviewed, 11 (n = 172) meta-analysed, random effects; I2 computed, value not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Al Khatib HK, Harding SV, Darzi J, Pot GK 2017, Eur J Clin Nutr 71:614-624; doi:10.1038/ejcn.2016.201; pmid:27804960

parameter: daily energy intake under partial sleep restriction to 5.5 h or less vs control (pooled)
value: SMD 0.37 (95% CI 0.21, 0.52); mean difference +204 kcal/d (95% CI 112, 295); more fat, protein and carbohydrate
range: 24 publications reviewed after risk-of-bias appraisal, 15 meta-analysed
citation: Fenton S, Burrows TL, Skinner JA, Duncan MJ 2021, J Hum Nutr Diet 34:273-285; doi:10.1111/jhn.12813; pmid:33001515

parameter: energy intake and hunger on the day after one night of about 4 h vs about 8 h sleep (acute)
value: +559 +/- 617 kcal (22%) on the day after restriction (P < 0.01); preprandial hunger higher before breakfast (P < 0.001) and dinner (P < 0.05); estimated physical activity also higher
range: randomised two-condition crossover, ad libitum meals; no certainty rating given
citation: Brondel L, Romer MA, Nougues PM, Touyarou P, Davenne D 2010, Am J Clin Nutr 91:1550-1559; doi:10.3945/ajcn.2009.28523; pmid:20357041

parameter: energy expenditure, energy intake and weight over 5 days of insufficient sleep and on recovery sleep
value: total daily energy expenditure +~5%; intake, especially after dinner, exceeded the energy needed for balance; weight +0.82 +/- 0.47 kg; moving to recovery sleep decreased intake, weight -0.03 +/- 0.50 kg
range: 14-15-day inpatient protocol; no certainty rating given
citation: Markwald RR, Melanson EL, Smith MR et al 2013, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A 110:5695-5700; doi:10.1073/pnas.1216951110; pmid:23479616

parameter: late-night and next-day energy intake after one night of total sleep deprivation vs one night of 4 h in bed (total vs partial loss)
value: late-night caloric intake comparable between restriction (22:00-04:00) and total deprivation (22:00-06:00) (p = 0.12); next-day intake moderately to substantially consistent within individuals across the two (ICC 0.34-0.75); men ate more late at night and the next day
range: within-subjects laboratory protocol; no certainty rating given
citation: Dennis LE, Spaeth AM, Goel N 2016, Nutrients 8:823; doi:10.3390/nu8120823; pmid:27999367

parameter: 24-h ad libitum energy intake at 19 °C vs 23.5 °C, and on the following day
value: +411 +/- 987 kcal/d (13%) while in the cold (P = 0.006); no difference the day after; the rise was not explained by cold-induced change in 24-h energy expenditure
range: controlled crossover, respiratory chamber with a vending-machine paradigm; no certainty rating given
citation: Unlu Y, Piaggi P, Stinson EJ et al 2025, Am J Clin Nutr 121:293-303; doi:10.1016/j.ajcnut.2024.12.013; pmid:39675563

parameter: hunger and ad libitum intake after 2.5 h at 18 °C vs 24 °C (the null reading for short mild cold)
value: no differences in hunger, food intake or satiety after mild cold; resting energy expenditure rose
range: crossover, two days about two weeks apart, blinded to the setting, in random order; no certainty rating given
citation: Langeveld M, Tan CY, Soeters MR et al 2016, Endocr Connect 5:65-73; doi:10.1530/ec-16-0004; pmid:26864459

parameter: ad libitum meal intake at rest after 30 min sternum-deep immersion in 16 °C vs 35 °C water vs 26 °C air
value: 2783 +/- 909 kJ after cold water vs 1817 +/- 862 kJ after thermoneutral water and 1894 +/- 233 kJ after air; no differences in appetite VAS; a core-temperature after-drop for 15 min after cold water
range: randomised crossover, at least 7 days apart; no certainty rating given
citation: Grigg MJ, Thake CD, Allgrove JE, Broom DR 2025, Physiol Behav 296:114914; doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2025.114914; pmid:40221072

parameter: buffet energy intake after 1 h of torso and foot heating (hot vest about 45 °C, foot bath about 43 °C) vs seated control
value: 849 +/- 317 vs 1025 +/- 343 kcal; mean difference -176 kcal (95% CI -329, -23), effect size -0.615; subjective appetite similar
range: randomised crossover, 28 days apart; no certainty rating given
citation: Li G, Watanabe D, Inoue Y et al 2026, Temperature (Austin) 13:214-226; doi:10.1080/23328940.2026.2672316; pmid:42282893

parameter: hunger and meal intake under nasal nicotine (15 ug/kg every 20 min for 2 h) vs placebo, after a caloric load or water (acute)
value: nicotine reduced hunger only after the caloric load, not after water; nicotine lowered caloric intake at the meal, not specifically of sweet high-fat foods
range: four sessions per subject; no certainty rating given
population: 10 male smokers and 10 male non-smokers, abstinent overnight
citation: Perkins KA, Epstein LH, Stiller RL et al 1991, Psychopharmacology (Berl) 103:103-109; doi:10.1007/bf02244083; pmid:2006236

parameter: appetite and plasma ghrelin 30 and 60 min after 2 mg nicotine gum vs placebo gum (acute)
value: appetite ratings decreased; plasma nonacylated ghrelin was not affected
range: double-blind randomised crossover, two studies; no certainty rating given
citation: Pilhatsch M, Scheuing H, Kroemer N et al 2014, Hum Psychopharmacol 29:384-387; doi:10.1002/hup.2405; pmid:24710917

parameter: weight gain in untreated quitters at 1 to 12 months after stopping smoking (pooled; the chronic withdrawal outcome)

parameter: free-living energy intake, laboratory appetite and ad libitum intake over two 12-week periods of lower- vs higher-glycaemic-index staple foods balanced for macronutrients, fibre and energy density (a long-term null)
value: free-living diets differed by 8.4 GI units (55.5 vs 63.9); no differences in energy intake, body weight or body composition; after test breakfasts (GI 52 vs 64, 2.5 MJ, matched available carbohydrate, fibre, protein and fat) no differences in hunger, fullness or ad libitum snack and lunch intake
range: randomised crossover, two consecutive 12-week periods, n = 19; the key foods supplied 48% of carbohydrate intake; no certainty rating given
population: overweight and obese women aged 34-65 y with moderate hyperinsulinaemia, BMI 25-47
citation: Aston LM, Stokes CS, Jebb SA 2008, Int J Obes (Lond) 32:160-165; doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803717; pmid:17923862

parameter: hunger, satiety and energy intake by doubly labelled water over 1 year of 30% calorie restriction with high- vs low-glycaemic-load diets
value: energy intake, weight, body fat and resting metabolic rate changes did not differ between groups; no effect of diet on hunger, satiety or satisfaction with the food; both groups ate more than provided (21% and 28% restriction at 3 months, 16% and 17% at 6 months, high and low load); weight change at 12 months -8.04 +/- 4.1% (high) vs -7.81 +/- 5.0% (low)
range: randomised controlled trial (CALERIE), n = 34; all food provided for 6 months, then self-administered for 6 months; the diets also differed in macronutrient composition (the low-load diet lower in carbohydrate and higher in fat and protein) and were matched for fibre, palatability and variety, so the contrast is not glycaemic load alone (the composition's direction read from the Tufts release of 2007-04-09; the full text not read, so no percentages are carried); no certainty rating given
population: healthy overweight adults aged 35 +/- 6 y, BMI 27.6
citation: Das SK, Gilhooly CH, Golden JK, Pittas AG, Fuss PJ, Cheatham RA et al 2007, Am J Clin Nutr 85:1023-1030; doi:10.1093/ajcn/85.4.1023; pmid:17413101

parameter: hunger and satiety over 6 months of isocaloric energy-restricted low-GI, high-GI and low-fat high-GI diets
value: BMI change -2.45 +/- 0.27 (low GI), -2.30 +/- 0.27 (high GI) and -1.43 +/- 0.27 (low fat, high GI) (P = 0.012; low vs high GI P = 1.000; low GI vs low fat P = 0.016); the three diets did not differ in their effects on hunger or satiety
range: randomised parallel trial (GLYNDIET), n = 122, 6 months; no certainty rating given
citation: Juanola-Falgarona M, Salas-Salvadó J, Ibarrola-Jurado N, Rabassa-Soler A, Díaz-López A, Guasch-Ferré M et al 2014, Am J Clin Nutr 100:27-35; doi:10.3945/ajcn.113.081216; pmid:24787494

parameter: dietary compensation and weight over 8 weeks of energy-matched fruit and vegetables added as beverages vs solids (the reading that the form difference was not significant)
value: dietary compensation 53% (beverage) vs 78% (solid); weight +1.95 +/- 0.33 kg (beverage) and +1.36 +/- 0.30 kg (solid), both P < 0.0005, difference between forms not significant; lean: solid 119% compensation and no significant gain (0.84 +/- 0.53 kg), beverage 43% (+1.61 +/- 0.44 kg); overweight and obese: solid 46% (+1.77 +/- 0.32 kg), beverage 61% (+2.22 +/- 0.47 kg)
range: randomised crossover, two 8-week periods with a 3-week washout, n = 34; no certainty rating given
citation: Houchins JA, Burgess JR, Campbell WW, Daniel JR, Ferruzzi MG, McCabe GP et al 2012, Obesity (Silver Spring) 20:1844-1850; doi:10.1038/oby.2011.192; pmid:21720441

parameter: challenge-meal intake and latency to the next eating event after a 400 kcal fruit preload as a solid vs a beverage, and appetite ratings after 8 weeks of each form
value: without a preload 535 +/- 40 and 542 +/- 32 g of the challenge meal were eaten; the solid preload cut it by 350 +/- 41 g and the beverage by 216 +/- 20 g (p = 0.005); latency to the next eating event not different between forms; total daily energy intake higher after the beverage in the obese (P < 0.001); hunger and fullness ratings stable over 8 weeks of either form
range: the same randomised crossover as Houchins 2012 (not independent of it), n = 34; preloads matched on fruit type, energy, carbohydrate, soluble fibre and volume: the solid preload was apple, grapes, dried apple and raisins with 470 g water, the beverage apple and grape juice with soluble fibre added and 150 g water; no certainty rating given
population: lean (n = 15) and overweight/obese (n = 19) adults with low habitual fruit and vegetable intake
citation: Houchins JA, Tan SY, Campbell WW, Mattes RD 2013, Int J Obes (Lond) 37:1109-1115; doi:10.1038/ijo.2012.183; pmid:23164702

parameter: satiety index of equal-energy portions of seven breads and its predictors
value: satiety index 100% (white bread) to 561%; mean satiety index correlated with test-meal intake at 120 min r = -0.88 (P < .01, n = 7) and total-day intake r = -0.72 (P < .05, n = 7); the strongest predictor of the breads' satiety index was portion size and thus energy density; glycaemic responses were not associated with fullness
range: within-subject repeated measures, n = 10; correlations across 7 breads; no certainty rating given
citation: Holt SH, Brand-Miller JC, Stitt PA 2001, J Am Diet Assoc 101:767-773; doi:10.1016/s0002-8223(01)00192-4; pmid:11478473

parameter: relation of satiety to postprandial glucose and insulin across 38 foods in 240 kcal portions (the satiety-index data set)
value: no significant relationship between satiety and plasma glucose or insulin responses; insulin AUC correlated negatively with ad libitum intake at 120 min; the authors read total carbohydrate and food structure, not glycaemic impact, as the stronger determinant of short-term satiety
range: the 38-food data set of Holt 1995 (S1226; not independent of it), separate groups of 11-13 per food category, random order within category; correlation values not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Holt SH, Brand Miller JC, Petocz P 1996, Eur J Clin Nutr 50:788-797; pmid:8968699

parameter: hunger and lunch intake after isocaloric instant oatmeal cooked in water vs a ready-to-eat oat cereal in milk with the water drunk beside it
value: breakfasts 363 kcal each (250 kcal cereal plus 113 kcal milk): oatmeal 66.8 g dry made with 360 g water, milk drunk; cereal 63.6 g in 307 g milk, 360 g water drunk; hunger-reduction AUC 10,615 +/- 727.15 vs 8,472.10 +/- 733.92 mm x min (p = 0.005); lunch intake 85 kcal lower after oatmeal (p = 0.012), weight of food eaten not different; per serving oatmeal 8.35 g protein, 6.68 g fibre, 1.67 g sugar vs cereal 4.54 g, 4.54 g, 20.43 g
range: randomised crossover, n = 48; funded by the Quaker Oats Center of Excellence and PepsiCo R&D, four authors PepsiCo employees; the water is inside the oatmeal but drunk beside the cereal, and protein, fibre and sugar differ, so the contrast is not fibre alone; no certainty rating given
citation: Rebello CJ, Johnson WD, Martin CK, Han H, Chu YF, Bordenave N et al 2016, J Am Coll Nutr 35:41-49; doi:10.1080/07315724.2015.1032442; pmid:26273900

parameter: satiety, gastric emptying and ad libitum lunch intake after isocaloric oatmeal vs corn flakes vs water
value: lunch intake lowest after oatmeal (p < 0.00001), and lower for overweight than lean subjects (p = 0.007); fullness AUC greatest (p = 0.00001) and hunger AUC lowest (p < 0.001) after oatmeal; acetaminophen peaked latest after oatmeal (slower gastric emptying, p = 0.046); magnitudes not in the abstract
range: three conditions in randomised sequence, n = 36 (18 lean, 18 overweight); lunch at 180 min; the abstract's P values are tests across the three conditions including water, and the oatmeal vs corn flakes contrast is the authors' conclusion without its own P in the abstract; serving weights not in the abstract; no certainty rating given
citation: Geliebter A, Grillot CL, Aviram-Friedman R, Haq S, Yahav E, Hashim SA 2015, Ann Nutr Metab 66:93-103; doi:10.1159/000365933; pmid:25612907

parameter: appetite and ad libitum lunch intake after baked, mashed or fried white potatoes vs isocaloric white bread with fat equalised (the potato's satiety-index ranking at equal energy and fat)
value: baked (288 kcal), mashed (283 kcal) and fried (280 kcal) potatoes and white bread (280 kcal), each with 13.7 g fat and 33.1 g available carbohydrate: appetite and lunch pizza intake lower than meal skipping (P < 0.001) for all four, but no difference among the potato treatments and white bread; cumulative intake not different among conditions
range: within-subject repeated measures in random order, n = 20 analysed (22 completed); funded by the Alliance for Potato Research and Education, one author on its advisory board; serving weights not reported in the text read; no certainty rating given
citation: Bellissimo N, Amalraj R, Lee JJ, Brett NR, Totosy de Zepetnek JO, Proteau S et al 2020, Nutrients 12:2606; doi:10.3390/nu12092606; pmid:32867083

parameter: subjective satiety and later ad libitum intake after four equi-energy potato meals vs an equi-energy pasta meal
value: a meal with fried French fries was rated more satiating than pasta on VAS; baked potato, mashed potato and wedges did not differ from pasta; all test meals had a comparable effect on energy intake at a later ad libitum meal
range: randomised crossover, n = 33; funding not read (abstract only); no certainty rating given
citation: Diaz-Toledo C, Kurilich AC, Re R, Wickham MS, Chambers LC 2016, J Am Coll Nutr 35:537-543; doi:10.1080/07315724.2015.1042560; pmid:27463259

parameter: daily ad libitum energy intake over 14 days of two ultra-processed diets matched for non-beverage energy density, palatability, portion size and energy served, and variety, that differ in texture-derived eating rate
value: intake 369 kcal/d (95% CI 221, 517) lower on the slow-eating-rate diet (main effect; 2331 vs 2641 kcal/d in the model corrected for fat served), consistent across the 14 days (diet x time P = 0.486) and not attributable to liking or macronutrient intake by the authors' analysis; as consumed, protein was 19 vs 15 EN% and fat EN% differed by 9 points; food eaten 1481 vs 1746 g/d; no notable differences in appetite ratings before or after meals; no weight difference; fat mass -0.43 kg on the slow diet
range: single-blind block-randomised crossover, two 14-day ad libitum periods with a 2-week washout, n = 41; no certainty rating given
population: healthy adults (21 men; age 27 y, BMI 23.4)
citation: Forde CG, Heuven LA, van Bruinessen M, Liu Z, Stieger M, de Graaf K et al 2026, Am J Clin Nutr 123:101122; doi:10.1016/j.ajcnut.2025.11.012; pmid:41314613

parameter: ad libitum buffet intake after 2 weeks of a eucaloric diet 81% vs 0% ultra-processed, matched for macronutrients, fibre, added sugar, diet quality and energy density (processing at matched energy density)
value: no effect of diet on buffet total kcal or grams, or on ultra-processed or non-ultra-processed intake, in the full sample (all p > 0.05); in an exploratory age subgroup intake rose after the ultra-processed diet in those aged 18-21 (p = 0.03, d = 0.79) but not 22-25
range: randomised crossover proof-of-concept controlled-feeding trial, two 14-day periods, 4-week washout, n = 27; a single buffet meal outcome; no certainty rating given
citation: Rego MLM, Leslie E, Schmall E, Capra B, Hudson S, Ahrens ML et al 2026, Obesity (Silver Spring) 34:344-356; doi:10.1002/oby.70086; pmid:41255123

parameter: body weight after more than 8 weeks of satiety-enhancing or hunger-reducing foods vs control in overweight and obesity (pooled), and how much of the weight change ad libitum intake explains
value: weight reduced by 3.60 kg (95% CI 1.05, 6.15) more than controls; in the two studies that tested it, the decrease in ad libitum energy intake explained 58% (12 weeks) and 23% (8 weeks) of the variation in weight loss (P < 0.001); robust acute appetite effects were as likely as sustained effects to be linked to better weight management
range: 12 studies from 517 papers, average 75 subjects exposed; Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (the verdict is not in the abstract); heterogeneous products; weight, not hunger, is the pooled outcome; no certainty rating given
citation: Hansen TT, Andersen SV, Astrup A, Blundell J, Sjödin A 2019, Obes Rev 20:983-997; doi:10.1111/obr.12854; pmid:30945414

parameter: appetite on low-fat (<= 30% energy) vs high-fat diets in randomised trials (systematic review, unpooled)
value: of seven studies on hunger, three reported a significantly lower hunger response on low fat; no effect on satiety, desire to eat or palatability; one study found a greater fall in total appetite score over 6 months; the authors find little or no additional benefit to appetite and call the evidence poor
range: 9 RCTs from 2471 records, no pooled estimate; RoB 2: 2 low risk, 4 some concerns, 2 high; no certainty rating given
citation: Razmpoosh E, Abdollahi S, Sikaroudi MK, Sangsefidi ZS, Zeraattalab-Motlagh S, Torabinasab K et al 2025, BMC Public Health 25:2264; doi:10.1186/s12889-025-23454-0; pmid:40604651

parameter: a GRADE-rated pooled estimate of higher- vs lower-protein diets on hunger or ad libitum energy intake over >= 8 weeks at equal energy density
range: named by Satiety research 2 Task 28; the 2026-10-09 search found no protein appetite meta-analysis with a GRADE or other certainty rating; the long-term trials with an appetite outcome (Leidy 2007, Westerterp-Plantenga 2004, Lejeune 2005) report direction only, and Kohanmoo 2020's 19 long-term trials (S1222) are null on ratings

parameter: the size of the hunger difference after calorie-matched low- vs high-energy-density meals sustained over weeks of dieting, pooled
range: named by Satiety research 2 Task 28; Ello-Martin 2007 and Buckland 2018 give direction and P only for hunger in the text read; no meta-analysis pools VAS hunger after calorie-matched energy-density contrasts over weeks
